entries.note: P0-05 F-stage (2026-09-01), fault/qualification hardening of the Shadow/Enforce Feature Gates mechanism. 4 real bugs found and fixed, each personally reproduced pre-fix and confirmed closed post-fix by an independent Reviewer using their own adversarial repro (not just re-reading the Writer's tests): (1) a hot-reload downgrade-authority gap -- resolveFeatureGate/evaluateFeatureGate had zero authority check, letting a settings or env override silently move a gate from its authored enforce floor to off/shadow; fixed with a hasKernelAdministrativeAuthority guard computed from the default/profile floor alone, deliberately left ctx-free per the standing BLOCKED-011 hard-stop (no epic may wire a real Trust Kernel enforcement point before the vendored Cordis Fiber fix lands; verified against docs/architecture/trust-kernel-boundary.md and .claude/goal.md verbatim). entries.note: P2-01 C-stage (2026-09-02), a unified Principal/Tenant/Run/Actor identity contract, security-foundation-tier per BLOCKED-022 (same release bar as P0-02's Trust Kernel; final --accept requires delegate ruling + explicit user confirmation, not covered by this freeze). Three independent review rounds, each finding real, blocking issues, none rubber-stamped: Round 1 REJECT -- isAdminPrincipal bypassable by a plain object literal (isAdmin: boolean with zero gating); fixed with a Branded-style adminGrant token + WeakSet membership check. Round 2 REJECT -- two more real findings: (a) the Round 1 fix itself had silently deleted an unrelated tsconfig.base.json path alias (dsh-evidence-format/types) by placing a hand-written subpath alias inside gen-tsconfig-paths.ts's generated region, breaking doc-typecheck; root-caused and fixed by moving it outside the region, matching an existing precedent already in the file. (b) A deeper bypass: WeakSet membership only proved a token was minted somewhere, never bound to a specific principal -- since PrincipalId/TenantId's brandString does zero runtime gating (return value as T), an attacker could mint a matching id/tenantId and reattach a stolen token. Fixed with WeakMap<AdminGrant, principal-object-reference> + === identity comparison, closing reconstruction-based forgery entirely; the disclosed limitation (a serialized/rehydrated principal is never === the original) was independently ratified as the correct fail-closed direction and PINned as a durable forward constraint (BLOCKED-025) for whichever future epic handles cross-process principal rehydration. An addendum added permanent regression tests proving the fail-closed serialization property (structuredClone and JSON round-trip). Round 3: ACCEPT -- every claim independently re-verified via direct source reading and real command execution (not re-reading self-reports), including an original adversarial reproduction beyond the shipped tests (reference-leakage audit: clean) and one new, explicitly non-blocking finding (in-place field mutation via TypeScript-only readonly with zero runtime enforcement -- Object.freeze recommended as a cheap follow-up, orthogonal to what this round committed to closing and unreachable today since nothing wires these objects into live authorization yet). entries.note:
P4-01's U2 remediation slice, package-suite half. The sign-off was WITHDRAWN (BLOCKED-183) because `advance`, `listNonTerminal` and `resume` had no production caller at all -- a refusal with no caller refuses nothing, and a registry nothing enumerates is not a restart path. These cases exist to make each of the three reachable and to fix what reaching them must look like.

TWO ARRANGEMENTS ARE DELIBERATELY DIFFERENT AND THE DIFFERENCE IS THE POINT. The three adoption cases mount the IN-MEMORY lease store, where two mounts own two maps and therefore CANNOT contend -- so they observe adoption and deliberately observe nothing about authority. `continues under a lease THIS mount was issued` and `opens NO Run for a restart inside the lease window` mount the SQLite store over a shared directory, which is the only arrangement in which a restart contends with itself. The first version of the epoch case ran against the in-memory store and failed with `expected +0 not to be +0`: the number was a second store's first answer, not adoption's. That is the same shape as SS12.35-2's own measurement -- per-Run work items made contention vacuous and acceptance[1] held for no reason -- and BLOCKED-189's rule about an instrument that does not depend on what it measures.

THE FOUR LIFECYCLE CASES READ THE DURABLE DOCUMENT, not in-memory state. Written the other way first, all four failed: `agent/disposed` is emitted synchronously and does not await its listeners, so the terminal transitions are still in flight when the agent handle's own dispose resolves. Reading back through a fresh `RunService.restore` also makes must[1]'s claim the stronger one -- the entries were persisted, not merely appended in memory.

`verifying` IS THE END DECISION OVER THIS PLUGIN'S FAILURE LEDGER AND NOT OUTPUT VERIFICATION. The path is `running -> verifying -> succeeded | failed` because the transition table admits no shortcut from `running` to `succeeded`; what the step reads is whether an unrecovered `agent/error` is this Run's last reported activity. Epic P7-05 owns the real meaning (its must[0] adds `accepted`, `rejected`, `needs-human` and `compensating` beside this state, its must[1] admits only execution-completed into `verifying`): the transition shape survives, the decision inside it is replaced. Recorded as a readiness note against P7-05 rather than as a defect.

acceptance[2]'s NEGATIVE HALF is frozen here and its positive second half is NOT implemented: `attachSession` has no caller, because a Run spanning sessions is writable under two independent authorities -- the lease's work item is the session and a Run's own writes present no lease at all. BLOCKED-196 holds it. The case whose subject is that absence exists so that wiring it without reading that entry reddens something.

THE CLEAN-UNLOAD TRIO IS THE DELEGATE'S THIRD FORM, after both of the shapes this lane put forward were rejected. Leaving a Run `running` on unload leaked a non-terminal Run and a held lease once per boot; TERMINATING it would have claimed work that is merely unfinished AND falsified P4-01's own frozen `restores the Runs an earlier mount left behind, rather than starting empty`, whose premise is that a clean unload leaves something restorable. `paused` keeps that case true and is the one legal Run state nothing had ever reached. The ruling's other half -- release the lease so a restart needs no lapse -- is NOT here: measured, `release` from that disposer throws, because the provider clears its handle synchronously while this disposer awaits the transition before it, and a fiber unload runs every disposer concurrently rather than in any order. BLOCKED-197 holds it, and `holds its work item past a clean unload too` freezes the measured behaviour so that closing the gap reddens something.

ONE CASE IN THIS ENTRY WAS INVERTED WHEN BLOCKED-197 CLOSED, and the title changed with it. It read `holds its work item past a clean unload too, so a restart waits out the lease either way` and was true: the hand-back sat after an `await`, so the lease provider had already cleared its handle. Moving the release above that await -- before `pauseRun` awaits anything -- makes it succeed, probed 10 of 10 before adoption. The case now asserts the release and the immediate continuation. What it really guards is a property of the VENDORED runtime that nothing promises: every disposer begins with `await Promise.resolve()`, so synchronous work at the top of ours wins by one microtask. A re-vendor that changes that prefix reddens this case, and the mutation for it -- moving the hand-back back below the first await -- reddens exactly this case and no other, 1 of 195.

sensitivityProof.mutationDescription: Twelve mutations in `packages/run/run/src/index.ts`, applied locally one at a time to the unmodified tree and reverted between each (the file restored from a byte copy before the next), then `pnpm exec vitest run packages/run/run --maxWorkers=2 --reporter=json`. All are constant/value/dependency replacements; no guard was deleted. (1) the mount enumeration widened past `listNonTerminal`; (2) the enumeration deferred past mount (`restoredAtMount = []`); (3) `adoptable` returning a Run whose `resume()` REFUSED (`decision.resumed || true`); (4) adoption disabled so `open` always mints (`continuing = undefined`); (5) a continued Run re-registered through `openForSession` (`if (true)`); (6) `startRun`'s `planning -> running` advance removed; (7) `endRun`'s `verifying` step removed so it asks for `running -> succeeded` directly; (8) `endRun` ignoring the failure ledger (always `succeeded`); (9) a Run that never ran advanced to `planning` instead of `cancelled`; (10) the clean-unload parking loop neutralized so the Run is left `running`; (11) `paused` removed from the states a first model step resumes from; (12) the clean unload advancing to `cancelled` instead of `paused`. (13) the lease hand-back moved from the top of `pauseRun` to after the `advance` it precedes, which is where it sat before BLOCKED-197 closed.
sensitivityProof.failureSummary:
Each reddened only its own cases out of 191. (1) RED 2 and (2) RED 2 -- the enumeration case and `opens NO Run for a restart inside the lease window`, which reads the enumeration to prove nothing was lost. (3) RED 1 -- `MINTS a fresh Run when the restored one is terminal`. (4) RED 3 and (5) RED 3 -- the three adoption cases; (3), (4) and (5) are each other's controls, so adoption is proved to be a DECISION rather than a default in both directions. (6) RED 2 -- both three-step lifecycle cases. (7) RED 3 -- both lifecycle cases and `leaves no non-terminal Run behind`, because `running -> succeeded` is illegal and the refusal leaves the Run non-terminal; this is the mutation the delegate named as required. (8) RED 1 -- `ends a session whose last reported activity was an unrecovered error at verifying -> failed`. (9) RED 1 -- `cancels a Run whose session was disposed before any model step`. (10) RED 2 and (12) RED 2 -- `PARKS a running Run at `paused` when the mount unloads cleanly` and `holds its work item past a clean unload too`; the two are each other's control, since one leaves the Run running and the other ends it, and only `paused` satisfies both cases. (11) RED 1 -- `takes a parked Run back to `running` at the next model step`. 

MUTATION (11) IS RECORDED WITH ITS OWN HISTORY: run before that case existed it reddened NOTHING out of 193, which is how the gap was found -- the `paused` branch had been added to `startRun` and no case observed it, so an adopted Run would have sat in `paused` forever while its agent worked. The case was written for the mutation, not the other way round. All mutations reverted; the committed tree is the unmutated one. (13) RED 1 -- `RELEASES its work item on a clean unload, so the next mount continues at once and waits out no lease`, which is the case standing in for an unload-ordering guarantee Cordis does not give.

entries.note:
The shipped-profile half of P4-01's U2 slice, and the half the withdrawal's ground actually asks for: a real `dsh-app-boot` boot of a real Loader composition, not a hand-built `ctx.plugin`.

A SECOND FIXTURE EXISTS BECAUSE A FROZEN CASE FORBIDS CHANGING THE FIRST. Adoption is keyed on the session, and `dsh-agent-loop`'s `agents[].sessionId` is optional -- without it every boot mints a session and each one correctly gets its own Run. The existing fixture has no id, and P4-01's own frozen case `opens a second, independent Run on the next boot over the same store, keeping the first` asserts exactly that its two boots are two sessions. `loader/p4-01-run-resumed/` therefore differs from `loader/p4-01-run/` by ONE line -- `sessionId: p4-01-durable-session` -- so the observation was added without touching a frozen case. Both fixture files are outside P4-01's declared file set and carry `files-overlay` reasons.

THE ENUMERATION CASE READS THE DRIVER'S STDOUT, and that is not a convenience. acceptance[0]'s enumerate half leaves NO trace in the durable document: the store records which Runs are non-terminal, never that this process asked. The driver prints the plugin's own answer (`restored N non-terminal Run(s)`), so the claim is observed rather than inferred from the state the plugin then acted on. Cold boot reports 0, warm boot reports 1.

THE WARM BOOT'S `1` IS ALSO A RECORDED LIMITATION, not a clean result. A Run does not reach a terminal state when the PROCESS ends: Cordis unloads this plugin before the agent registry disposes its agents, so the `agent/disposed` listener that drives the terminal transitions is already gone. Zero module/syntax errors; C+P+U's 148 frozen cases are untouched -- this stage edits no landed case, adds one new fixture file, and its fix-round touches exactly one production file. METHOD: the four defects were reproduced by a throwaway probe spec run against the landed code BEFORE any case was designed, so every RED case names a defect that was observed rather than one that was reasoned about; the probe was deleted and never committed. DEFECT 2 IS THE SERIOUS ONE. Two concurrent RunService.advance calls out of one state BOTH returned accepted: true -- one to planning, one to cancelled -- and the durable log ended with only null->accepted@0 and accepted->cancelled@1. An accepted transition vanished from an append-only log, and the service admitted two mutually exclusive exits from one state, violating must[1] and acceptance[1] simultaneously. Root cause: advance reads this.registered(id) synchronously, then awaits store.put, so two callers both decide against the same pre-transition Run and the later write wins. The frozen case uses verifying -> succeeded / failed because both are legal out of verifying and both terminal, so in EITHER application order exactly one may be accepted -- the assertion is order-independent, not a race the case happens to win. Provider stage proved acceptance[0] over a store this repo's own code wrote and nothing disturbed; the happy path was never the risk. The other three RED defects: (1) createFileRunStore's temp path is `${path}.${process.pid}.tmp`, so two stores over one path IN ONE PROCESS collide on that exact name and the second rename fails ENOENT -- observed, not theorized; (3) read() does `JSON.parse(text) as RunStoreDocument` with no validation past the version field, so a store naming state 'not-a-state' and ownerId 'some-ui-session' restores verbatim, is returned by listNonTerminal(), and resume() answers resumed: true -- a Run in no state at all offered for resumption, at a durable/file boundary the repo rules require validating; (4) appendRunEvent derives seq from run.events.length, so a log whose only entry is seq 7 appends at seq 1 -- a backwards seq in an append-only log. Defect (4) is closed by REFUSING the gapped log at load in src/index.ts, deliberately NOT by editing src/events.ts, so no landed C-stage case is disturbed. THE THREE CHARACTERIZATION CASES pass at RED and pin fault handling that is already correct (corrupt JSON refused loudly; an unsupported format version refused by name; an interrupted write's leftover temp file ignored while the complete document still restores). Frozen on Supervisor ruling, over this Writer's own recommendation of a 100%-RED freeze: an unprotected correct behaviour is one refactor away from an unnoticed regression, and freezing the titles makes the frozen-titles gate protect them. The CHARACTERIZATION: prefix follows the `control:` precedent; note that no earlier F entry used a machine-readable prefix, though P0-02.F did mark such cases in prose inside the title ('this is the known, accepted gap, not a bug in pinTrustKernel') and P2-01.F froze an unlabelled pass-at-RED control ('a well-formed, non-empty chain is completely unaffected by the guard'). The prefix extends that practice; it does not contradict it. APPROVED PATH PATCH P4-01-F-durable-registry-fault-surface, expressed as WIDENING not substitution: the declared F file packages/run/run/tests/state-machine.spec.ts keeps its work, and packages/run/run/src/index.ts is added. The declared spec covers src/state-machine.ts and src/events.ts, which are pure functions over caller-supplied values with no file, process, or shared state -- after C's exhaustive 10x10 sweep there is no fault left to inject there. Every remaining fault lives in the durable/concurrent layer, which is src/index.ts. Precedent confirms an F stage may fix what its own fault cases prove: P0-05.F's files include packages/migration/feature-gates/src/index.ts and P2-01.F's include packages/core/agent-loop/src/runtime-context.ts, both production source. This stage extends no behaviour beyond what its four cases prove; anything larger would be a C re-freeze via supersession. coordinator.ts DECLARED-BUT-UNMODIFIED, approved, and P's reasoning holds UNCHANGED at F -- worth stating because a later reader will ask whether F should have differed. Every PersistenceCoordinator entry point is keyed on SessionId (loadStored, append, prepare, load, inspect, borrowSession, readFrom), records are SessionEvents under a SessionHeader gated by SESSION_FORMAT_VERSION (coordinator.ts:94-96), and states/chains/retirements are all Map<SessionId, ...> (lines 640-651). There is no Run fault to inject into a file with no notion of a Run. A declared file left unmodified is a scope ceiling honoured, not a quota missed. FINDING, recorded because the absence is itself evidence: the registry declares fixtures.fault as tests/first100/fixtures/P4-01.fault.spec.ts and NO SUCH FILE EXISTED on disk -- only the U-stage composition fixture did. This stage creates the declared path rather than inventing a new one. CROSS-PROCESS LIMITATION STATED, NOT IMPLIED AWAY: the fix serializes writers per resolved store path WITHIN one process, following PersistenceCoordinator's own `chains = new Map<SessionId, Promise<unknown>>()` precedent (coordinator.ts:651). Two SEPARATE PROCESSES writing one store path still race, and closing that needs file locking, which is out of this stage's scope. The fix must not be read as delivering cross-process safety. The ENOENT in the RED output is a diagnostic observation, never an assertion. Exactly 4 of the 15 are RED and they are the only cases asserting behaviour the landed code does not have; the other 11 pass on arrival and are frozen as regression protection, titled `fault[...]`, `control:`, or `characterization:` so the distinction survives in the test names themselves. This is deliberate and matches precedent: P0-02.F froze the ctx.trustKernel poisoning cases as the known accepted gap and P2-01.F froze `a well-formed, non-empty chain is completely unaffected by the guard`, both already-green at their RED. The `control:`/`characterization:` prefix follows P1-09.U, which is where that prefix precedent actually is -- no landed F entry uses one. FAULT A -- acceptance[0] is literally false today, not merely unproven. solvePluginGraph's own JSDoc promises `the result does not depend on array order (acceptance[0])`. Two manifests sharing a pluginId break that promise: comparePluginId returns 0, Array.prototype.sort is stable, and input order survives into the output. Measured on the landed code: the same two-manifest set in the two orders produced planIds `[{active},{blocked}]` and `[{blocked},{active}]`, DUPORDER-EQUAL false, and RDUPORDER-EQUAL false through resolveActivatedGraph too. A documented guarantee the code does not provide is worse than an undocumented gap, because every downstream caller is entitled to rely on it; and the resulting plan carries two contradictory rows for one plugin identity, which the epic's gate (`Only a unique solved lock/ABI/schema/capability plan activates`) does not admit. FAULT A's intended GREEN is fail-loud, and that is a judgment call worth naming. The two candidate fixes are (i) reject a duplicated pluginId at the graph boundary and (ii) make the ordering total so the plan is at least deterministic. (ii) was rejected: a totally-ordered plan still contains two rows for one identity, so it satisfies acceptance[0] while still violating the gate's uniqueness requirement. (i) is chosen -- manifests reach solvePluginGraph from package.json parsing, an untrusted durable/file boundary, so a duplicated package identity in one profile is misconfiguration, and the repo rule is that misconfiguration fails loud. The frozen cases assert a throw naming the duplicated id. FAULT B -- one plugin's self-contradictory manifest takes down the whole graph, with false attribution. findProviderConstraintContradictions never checks that the requires-site and the excludes-site belong to different manifests, so a single manifest declaring both requires-provider P and excludes-provider P on the same sole provider returns solvable:false. Measured: with `provider`, `healthy` and `selfcontra` in the graph, F2-SOLVABLE false -- the two healthy plugins receive no activation at all, directly contradicting the epic's rollback clause (`incompatible candidate stays inactive`, not `the boot fails`). Worse, both core entries blame `selfcontra` while their detail strings read `another manifest's excludes-provider constraint` when no other manifest exists. must[2] requires a minimal unsat core; a misattributed core is worse than an unattributable one, because it sends the reader to an innocent plugin. The fix is to delete the wrong branch, not repair it: admissibleProviders already handles this case locally and blocks only selfcontra with provider-constraint-violation. PATCH A SCOPE, expressed as widening not substitution -- the declared spec file keeps its work. This is a genuine must[1] violation rather than a policy decision: must[1] ("官方保留 namespace 不可被第三方声明") is stated UNCONDITIONALLY, and must[2] says an override needs an explicit replace contract AND policy -- it does not say policy suspends must[1]. `allowReplace` defaulting to false limits exposure; it does not make the bypass acceptable. REACHABLE IN PRODUCTION, PROVEN ON THE REAL PATH, NOT ONLY IN THE PURE MODEL: `ToolRuntime.replace` (packages/core/tools/src/index.ts:1221) forwards straight to `requestReplace` with the deployment policy and throws only on `!decision.admitted`, so any STATICALLY loaded third-party cordis.yml entry -- exactly the third party must[1] names -- can take a reserved tool name. Not reachable from a DYNAMIC package: cordis-host-runner's `sandboxTools` façade exposes `register` only, never `replace`. RED STATE, CONFIRMED BY PARSING THE JSON REPORTER (--reporter=json --outputFile), NOT CONSOLE OUTPUT: 35 discovered, 33 pass, 2 FAIL, zero module/syntax/import-resolution errors. The two reds are the two halves of the finding and nothing else -- the pure-model case fails `AssertionError: expected true to be false` on `takeover.admitted`, and the real-registry case fails `Error: expected the registration to be refused`, i.e. `evil-plugin` genuinely became the owner of `dsh.core.read_file` in a real ToolRuntime tree. expectExit=0 is the GREEN target. WHICH CASES ARE RED AND WHICH ALREADY HOLD, DISCLOSED RATHER THAN IMPLIED: 2 of the 8 frozen cases are red (the two named above). The other 6 pass at this RED tree and are regression pins on properties that are correct today but were never exercised -- three of them differ from a Contract case in a way that looks cosmetic and is not. (a) The Contract stage's load-order case ran against an EMPTY registry, so the ORDER of the reserved-namespace and collision checks was never exercised; reversing them would report a naming clash where the real refusal is a namespace one, and the reason string is what the Usage stage's registrants assert on. (b) The Contract stage's cross-plugin token case used a DIFFERENT plugin's token; the forged-token case here reproduces the real owner's mint prefix exactly (`mintOwnershipToken` builds `${pluginIdentity}:${randomUUID()}` and a plugin identity is public), so it pins that revocation compares the whole token rather than the identity it names. The 4 failing cases require no not-yet-existing export in order to compile, so the RED is assertion-level throughout. THE DEFECT: downgradeTrust never checks direction. Called with a raising target it returns a record at 'trusted-execute' with no Principal, no isHostUserPrincipal check and no TrustUpgradeAuditRecord, reporting revokedKinds: [] -- must[2] (an upgrade requires host-user interaction and an audit) bypassed through acceptance[2]'s own entry point. Symmetrically, requestTrustUpgrade accepts a LOWERING target, reports upgraded: true, writes an audit record for a demotion, and stamps grantedBy onto an 'untrusted' record -- which types.ts documents as impossible (an untrusted record carries no grantor). REACHABILITY, STATED SO NEITHER MISREADING IS INVITED: downgradeTrust has NO production caller (grep -rn downgradeTrust --include='*.ts' packages apps tests finds only src/index.ts, its own JSDoc, and this spec), so NO LIVE EXPLOIT WAS DEMONSTRATED. requestTrustUpgrade's lowering path IS reachable: WorkspaceEntity.upgradeTrust(target, hostPrincipal) passes target through untouched, so upgradeTrust(ws, 'untrusted', hostUser) really does mint an untrusted-with-grantor record today. The reachable half manufactures exactly the input that makes the unreachable half dangerous, and a shipped state-machine transition that raises trust with no principal, no host-user check and no audit record is a defect whatever calls it today. NOT hypothetical, and NOT a proven live exploit. PLANNED FIX (Step 2, under the widening granted for workspace-trust/src/{index,types}.ts): downgradeTrust THROWS on a raising target and requestTrustUpgrade REFUSES a non-raising one through a new TrustUpgradeDenialReason member. The asymmetry is forced, not stylistic: downgradeTrust's success shape cannot become a discriminated union without breaking C's frozen cases, which read result.record and result.revokedKinds directly, so the refusal there must be a throw while requestTrustUpgrade already has a refusal union to extend additively. F1, RANKED BY SEVERITY (must[3] + validation[1] '测试跨 tenant/scope 读取'). Three categories, worst first:

A tenant could overwrite another tenant's durable data and be told it succeeded. This is a third category, not a facet of the read leak, and it outranks it.
  (2) CROSS-TENANT DESTRUCTION — forget() under tenant-b deleted tenant-a's record.
  (3) CROSS-TENANT DISCLOSURE — export/query/get returned tenant-a's content verbatim to tenant-b.

So this was NOT a forgotten tenant filter but an ABSENT filter — no dimension of MemoryScope bounded any read or write, which is exactly why must[3] names four dimensions rather than one.
  createLocalReferenceMemoryProvider and createFakeMemoryProvider are shipped, exported production factories in packages/memory/memory/src/index.ts, not test doubles; neither stored nor filtered by MemoryScope. F2 (kept separate from F1, not folded in): capRecords with a negative maxRecords runs slice(0, -1) and drops only the LAST record -- measured n=-1 returned 2 of 3 records while reporting truncated: true. M1 (skip the corrupt row and keep reading): 3 red -- both stop-at-first-corruption enforcement cases plus the DEFECT case that depends on evidence being returned at all. M2 (collapse started/not-started to always-started): exactly 1 red, the not-started case, and only that one. TWO DEFECTS RECORDED, NOT FIXED, because both fixes lie outside this stage's declared files. (1) readSessionLogWithRepair copies the caller-supplied raw row into evidence with no bound of its own; CorruptedLogEvidence.raw is documented as truncated to 512, but that truncation exists only in the JSONL scanner, so any other producer hands through an unbounded row -- a 100KB corrupt row is retained whole. (2) The entry point opens with `void sessionId`, so evidence can never name which session was corrupt. Separately, and outside this stage entirely: the JSONL scanner's own 512 limit is applied with String.slice, which cuts UTF-16 code units rather than bytes -- 512 units of CJK is 1536 bytes, 3x the documented cap, and a cut can strand a lone surrogate that becomes U+FFFD when re-encoded, corrupting the corruption evidence. Owner is packages/session/session-persistence-jsonl.

THE ESCAPE HATCH'S VALIDATOR IS WEAKER THAN THE RULE IT GUARDS. layering.md rule 5 calls the exemption store one 'a gate cannot widen its own escape hatch'. Five DEFECT cases record entries that satisfy validateExemptedCycle while recording nothing actionable: a whitespace-only reason, owner, or adrNote (the checks test `=== ''`, which one space defeats); a cycle naming one package twice (`cycle.length < 2` counts entries, not distinct packages); an adrNote that is prose rather than the repo-relative Agent Note path must[3] requires; and the impossible calendar date 2026-02-31, which matches the ISO shape while Date.parse returns a number for it rather than NaN, so the NaN guard never fires. CALIBRATION OF THE REAL-REPOSITORY VERDICT. The Usage stage asserts the real repo reports zero violations. An always-zero verdict and a broken verdict produce identical reports, so three cases calibrate it: the real scan reaches real input (>200 packages, >1000 edges, zero unclassified); its reporting path is live on that input (findings non-empty, produced by the same edge walk and classification as violations, so an empty violations list is a measurement rather than a dead path); and the same entry point on a fixture root reports a real kernel-upward-dependency violation, so zero distinguishes this repository from a function that never reports.

kernel refusals: acceptance[1] grants the kernel no exception, so a kernel upward edge is asserted to stay a violation even as the narrow event-type kind, with a non-kernel control on the identical edge proving the case measures the kernel rule and not the allowance.

They passed at runtime because classifyEdge reads only nature, fromLayer and toLayer, so malformed objects produced correct verdicts. Repo-wide typecheck rejected them. A green suite over objects that do not satisfy their own interface is why the package-level build is the faster check and never the sufficient one.

P4-05 C-stage. FROZEN BEFORE FIRST EXECUTION -- neither the module nor its spec has been run, so these titles are predictions.

WHY A NEW MODULE: `AgentStatus` in runtime-types.ts is a two-value runtime flag ('idle' | 'running') that cannot express the distinctions a supervisor needs. A run waiting on a tool and a run waiting on a human are both 'running' there, yet only one can ever proceed unattended -- so must[0]'s ten states are added alongside that flag, not as a replacement.

TWO PROPERTIES MADE STRUCTURAL RATHER THAN LEFT TO CALLERS. must[1]'s reason/runId/epoch are REQUIRED FIELDS of AgentTransition, so a transition lacking them is not a constructible value. acceptance[0]'s stale-worker half is decided by lease epoch alone -- no clock, no heartbeat, nothing a retrying stale worker can forge.

CHECK ORDER IS DELIBERATE AND ASSERTED: identity, then authority, then legality, then completeness. A stale worker proposing an ILLEGAL edge is refused for staleness, not illegality, so it never learns whether its edge would have been legal on a lifecycle it no longer owns. One case pins exactly that pair.

THREE MODELLING DECISIONS THE CASES PIN, each of which could reasonably have gone the other way: `cancelling` is EXCLUDED from the non-consuming set because a draining run still holds its slot, so a supervisor that treated it as idle would reclaim resources in use; terminal states have NO outgoing edges at all, including to `orphaned`, so a reclaim sweep cannot rewrite a finished run; and `orphaned` may NOT resume directly as `running` but must pass through `starting`, because starting is what issues the new epoch and resuming directly would keep the dead worker's epoch alive -- which is the very value acceptance[0]'s staleness test compares.

Controls accompany the negative-space cases: the empty-reason refusals are paired with the same edge carrying a real reason, and the stale-epoch refusal with the same proposal at the current epoch, so each refusal measures the property named rather than a decider that refuses everything.

P4-05 F-stage, appended to the Contract stage's spec file, which the registry declares as this stage's sole deliverable. All 20 Contract titles remain present and unmodified -- asserted before freezing, not assumed.

HONEST FREEZE PROVENANCE, stated because it is mixed: the 20 Contract cases were already frozen and run under P4-05.C. Six fault cases were written and run in this session before this entry existed. TWO cases -- the epoch-advancement pair in the final describe -- HAVE NEVER BEEN EXECUTED, and their outcome was unknown when this entry was written.

WHY THOSE TWO EXIST: BLOCKED-079 recorded a mutation that added a direct orphaned -> running edge and reddened ONLY the prohibition itself, while every stale-epoch assertion kept passing. The prohibition was asserted; the property it protects was not. The delegate's correction, accepted: that is not a case for deferring to P4-07, because the mutation named an unasserted property WITHOUT revealing whether asserting it would pass -- so the result is genuinely unknown, which is the definition of a Fault-stage target rather than a transcription. The distinction from P0-08.U's post-hoc freeze is exact: there the result had already been observed.

The property splits across two epics and only one half is here. The state machine's half -- the reclaim path can carry a greater epoch through, and once it has, the previous holder's proposals are stale -- is asserted. The half requiring a real lease store to ISSUE the greater epoch is P4-07's.

A DEFECT FOUND AND NOT FIXED: decideTransition reads LEGAL_TRANSITIONS[transition.from] unguarded, so a corrupt lifecycle naming an unknown state throws a TypeError instead of returning a refusal -- a caller handling decisions but not exceptions crashes on a log written by a newer build. The guard belongs in the Contract stage's frozen file.

A FAR-FUTURE EPOCH IS ADMITTED, asserted as correct rather than overlooked: staleness is strictly-older, and a worker holding a NEWER lease is the legitimate owner. Refusing it would strand a run whose lease was reissued while a supervisor held a stale view -- the opposite failure from the one acceptance[0] names.

REACHABILITY is proven by a real traversal: every state is reachable from queued, so no state is declared and stranded, which would look covered while being dead.

acceptance[2] is NOT asserted anywhere. It needs agent-run state surviving a restart, which this repository lacks; the lock names P4-07.

P8-01 C-stage. FROZEN BEFORE FIRST EXECUTION -- the spec has never been run, so these titles are predictions. The three source modules were written in an earlier commit that explicitly disclaimed any cell and any freeze; this entry is that pipeline step, performed before the suite's first execution.

SUBJECT-EXISTENCE CHECKED BEFORE STARTING, per the rule that saved a lane on P2-03's plugin-rpc: `packages/sdk/protocol` exists, `initialize` is a live method with real InitializeParams/InitializeResult types, and per-message schemaVersion negotiation through @deepseek-ai/dsh-schema-registry already ships. So must[0]'s handshake has a real subject to extend, unlike a clause naming a surface that does not exist.

WHAT THE EXISTING HANDSHAKE DOES NOT ANSWER, and why this is not duplication: schemaVersion negotiation answers 'can this build read this message'. It does not answer 'can these two peers work together at all', which is what a client needs BEFORE sending a task rather than after a field silently vanishes. Version ranges answer the second question.

HIGHEST rather than lowest mutually supported version, asserted deliberately: lowest would silently hold both peers at the oldest shape either has ever supported, which is how a capability stops being used without anyone deciding to stop using it. Symmetry is asserted directly -- a rule that is not symmetric gives two peers different answers about the same pair.

must[2]'s TWO refusal reasons are kept distinct because a peer can act on the difference: unknown means version skew, unsupported means a real gap. An unknown OPTIONAL capability is IGNORED rather than refused, which is the entire purpose of the mandatory/optional split, and ignored ones are RECORDED rather than dropped so a peer can see what went unused.

THE FINGERPRINT'S TWO REQUIREMENTS PULL OPPOSITE WAYS and the tension is the design problem: acceptance[2] wants stability, acceptance[3] wants sensitivity. The line drawn is wire-visible shape only -- declaration order does NOT move it, because a fingerprint reporting false drift on a refactor stops being consulted, while a version bump, an added method, a removed resource type, and a method-versus-event name collision all DO move it. Fields are length-prefixed so a name containing the separator cannot forge another surface's digest.

validation[1], deliberate breakage: withdrawing a mandatory capability from the supported set turns an accepted handshake into a refusal, and withdrawing it from the KNOWN set changes the refusal REASON -- so the two failure modes stay distinguishable rather than collapsing into one. validation[2], cross-implementation agreement: the Python half cannot run here, and no assertion pretends otherwise. What IS asserted is the property that makes two implementations able to agree at all -- the negotiated profile is a pure function of the fixture, identical across repeated derivations, with no dependence on ambient state or invocation count. A profile that varied per call could not be matched by any second implementation. The fixture pins its expected profile as LITERALS rather than by comparing the functions to themselves, so a Python port has a concrete target; a self-comparison would give it nothing to match.

WHY: BLOCKED-085. The original freeze contained a case asserting that length-prefixing prevents a name containing the field separator from forging another surface. Mutation M2 removed length-prefixing entirely and reddened NOTHING. Computed rather than guessed: the fixtures {name:'a:b',schemaId:'x'} and {name:'a',schemaId:'b:x'} concatenate to "a:bx1.0" and "ab:x1.0", which differ whether or not fields are prefixed, because moving the colon also moves it relative to its neighbours. The new case is the real collision: the BOUNDARY moves while the character sequence does not. Unprefixed, 'ab'+'c' and 'a'+'bc' both absorb as "abc", so no unprefixed hash can separate them. Its outcome was unknown when written -- the implementation was expected to prefix correctly, but expected is not known, and had it failed that would have been a genuine defect M2 already proved the suite could not catch.

WRITTEN TWICE, and the first version is the reason for the second. The first draft asserted properties of literal objects: it built a reply, then checked that the literal contained what had just been written into it. Every one of those cases would have passed with the client's reader DELETED -- BLOCKED-085's defect exactly, committed within an hour of recording it. Rewritten so every case spawns the fake runtime, performs a real `initialize`, and reads what the client actually returns.

fake-runtime.ts gains one env flag, `FAKE_NEGOTIATE`, carrying the JSON to merge into the initialize result. One flag rather than one per case, so a complete, partial and malformed negotiation are the same code path with different data -- and a case cannot pass because its own bespoke server branch was written to make it pass.

WHAT ONLY EXISTS AT THE BOUNDARY: a complete negotiation reaches the caller intact (the client previously rebuilt its result from serverInfo alone and discarded the rest); an absent negotiation is admitted with the field ABSENT rather than empty, since absence means the peer predates negotiation and reading it as an empty agreement would refuse every older server; a malformed range is dropped rather than repaired; and a partially-formed negotiation is dropped WHOLE, because a caller would treat the fields that did arrive as authoritative.

P4-06 P-stage. First freeze for this cell.

PRE-FLIGHT, run before the first line: does this repository have a transaction boundary that could satisfy must[0]'s 'commit the domain event and the outbox record in one transaction'? It has one, and it is NARROWER than the clause. Measured, not assumed: the write-ERROR path is atomic (appendLines stats the file and rollbackAppend restores the pre-batch size), and materialize-plus-first-batch is atomic by appendBatch's stated contract, but the CRASH path is not -- recovery truncates to `truncateTo: committedBytes`, the last COMPLETE JSONL record, not the batch boundary. A crash inside a two-entry batch can therefore keep the domain event and drop the outbox record, which is the unrecoverable direction. Filed as BLOCKED-089 before building.

WHAT THIS CELL ACTUALLY DELIVERS, at its measured strength: enqueueAll removes a DIFFERENT and genuinely live hazard. startWrite splices the whole pending queue, so two separate enqueue calls with a write starting between them land in different batches. The first frozen case demonstrates that split happening against the real controller, because a mechanism that prevents nothing is worth nothing. One batch instead of two is real and is NOT 'transactional'; describing it as transactional would repeat the day's recurring defect of stating a mechanism above what it was measured to do.

TEST PLACEMENT: SessionWriteBehind is internal to session-persistence and not exported from its root, so the batching proof lives in that package's own suite against the real controller, and message-bus tests only what it owns -- that commitWithOutbox reaches the sink as one ordered group and refuses the empty case. The first draft imported the controller across the package boundary and failed to resolve; the boundary was respected rather than worked around by widening exports.

EQUIVALENT MUTANT, recorded deliberately: replacing enqueueAll's single push with a loop reddens NOTHING, and that is correct rather than a gap. Indivisibility comes from the method never awaiting -- a write can only begin at a suspension point, and there is none inside the group. Writing that mutation is what revealed the JSDoc had credited the wrong mechanism (the single push rather than the absence of a suspension point), and the comment was corrected. A surviving mutant is not automatically a missing test, but it always means the stated mechanism deserves rereading.

P4-06 F-stage. First freeze for this cell. UNLIKE the C and U stages, BOTH declared files are genuinely this epic's -- crash.e2e.spec.ts (at its adjudicated path) and outbox.ts. No name collision here, checked rather than assumed.

validation[0] asks for a SYSTEMATIC fault matrix over at least 12 boundaries. The boundaries are enumerated as DATA and driven by one runner, and the count is asserted against the clause's floor -- a hand-written case per boundary would let one be deleted while every remaining case still passed, so the floor is what makes the enumeration checkable. 18 boundaries, all distinct titles (also asserted).

validation[2] asks that dead-letter produce a clear alert. The alert is a separate channel from the returned DispatchReport, because a report tells the CALLER and an alert must reach someone who is not reading the return value -- a dead-lettered message has stopped being retried and nothing else will mention it again. Three properties are pinned: it fires with the record and reason, it fires only AFTER the state is persisted (an alert describing a state that failed to persist would send an operator after a record the log does not show as dead), and it does NOT fire on an ordinary failed send.

validation[1]'s 10,000 redeliveries were already covered in the C stage and are not duplicated here.

TWO BOUNDARIES WERE FIXED BEFORE FREEZING, and the mutation is what found them. Boundaries 10 and 11 asserted that a receipt naming another message id or epoch is refused, but they built the record in `pending` state -- from which acking is an ILLEGAL TRANSITION anyway. Both threw, both passed, and dropping the epoch check entirely reddened NOTHING: the assertions were satisfied by the state machine while claiming to test the identity check. Rebuilt on a `sent` record, where acking would be legal, so the only thing that can refuse is the check under test. A forged-HIGH epoch is refused as stale: epochs are issued only by the store, so one above the current did not come from it, and admitting it would make a forgery the strongest authority in the system -- the fail-closed direction is refusing the unknown, not accepting the larger. P4-07 P-stage. First freeze for this cell.

The store is the SOLE issuer of epochs, which is what makes the Contract stage's checkFencing meaningful: a token can carry only an epoch this store handed out, so refusing anything that is not the item's current epoch refuses every forgery too.

THREE DECISIONS carry their own cases and each names the failure it prevents. Epoch counters are PER WORK ITEM -- a shared counter would let activity on one item advance another's, and epoch 7 of item A says nothing about item B. A heartbeat moves the deadline and does NOT issue a new epoch, because bumping it would fence the holder out of its own work. Renewal of an already-expired lease is refused rather than granted: the scheduler may already have handed that item to someone else, so reviving a lapsed holder IS the two-masters state.

acceptance[2] is treated as contract rather than as an error path. While unavailable, acquire refuses with 'store-unavailable' and reclaimable returns nothing -- stop-work in both directions. The reason is a distinct tag rather than a null result because 'nobody holds this' and 'I cannot tell you who holds this' must not look alike to a scheduler; reporting an item free during an outage is exactly how the same work reaches a second worker. A positive control (the store resuming once available again) sits beside the three refusal cases, because without it a store stuck permanently unavailable would satisfy every one of them.

entries.note:
P4-07 U-stage. First freeze for this cell. dispatch.ts is a REAL subject here, unlike P4-06's use of the same file -- see the C-stage freeze note.

THE GAP THIS STAGE CLOSES WAS MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED. advanceAgentLifecycle cannot enforce authority, and the reason is structural: NOTHING ISSUES THE LIFECYCLE'S EPOCH. decideTransition refuses only a strictly OLDER epoch and then adopts whatever the proposal carried, so the epoch a lifecycle holds is only ever the last one a caller asserted. A worker proposing epoch 9999 against a lifecycle at 1 is admitted AND becomes the new authority. A CHARACTERIZATION case pins that behaviour directly, so the fenced entry point is measured against a real hole rather than an imagined one.

P4-05'S CONTRACT WAS NOT EDITED. The gap is closed from outside: checkFencing runs against the store's current lease first, so the epoch reaching decideTransition is one the STORE issued rather than one the caller chose. The two staleness rules stay deliberately different and this is not a contradiction -- decideTransition compares against a lifecycle that LEARNS its epoch from transitions, so it must admit a newer one; checkFencing compares against a store that ISSUES epochs, so anything but the current one is a forgery. Running the issuer's check first makes the lifecycle's more permissive rule unreachable by an attacker.

ORDER IS PART OF THE CONTRACT, and one case exists only to pin it. A token that is BOTH fenced and proposing an illegal edge must report 'fenced'. This applies the principle already stated in decideTransition's own JSDoc -- ordering authority first means 'a stale worker never learns whether its proposed edge would have been legal'. Running fencing after the lifecycle decision leaks exactly that to a worker with no authority to ask. The first draft of this suite had no such case and the reordering mutation reddened ZERO; the case was added rather than the mutation dismissed as equivalent.

P4-05's lifecycle types were internal to dsh-agent and are now exported, because P4-07's fenced entry point takes them as parameters and an outside caller could not otherwise name what it must pass. Same shape as P8-01's Provider stage, where a missing re-export WAS the stage's substance.

PRE-FLIGHT on validation[2] ('stale token rejection is written to audit'). The subject is HALF present, measured rather than assumed: TrustKernel.auditAppend is literally `(_entry: TrustKernelAuditEntry): void => {}` and the kernel exposes NO read member at all -- by design, since a function type with that signature cannot expose one. So an appended entry is unobservable to anything, a test included. The producible half is real and is built: describeFencingRejection returns a complete record naming who was refused, who was current, and why. It deliberately carries no signature, key, or secret material -- the record describes an authorization DECISION, and quoting the token's credentials would leak them into whatever backs the audit chain. A KNOWN GAP case states plainly which half is proved.

RESIDUAL PINNED AS A MEASURED FACT, per the delegate's ruling, and it is TWO facts kept apart. decideTransition adopting a proposal's epoch is permissive but harmless alone; what makes it REACHABLE is that advanceAgentLifecycle is a PUBLIC EXPORT of dsh-agent, so any consumer -- including a third-party plugin, in a product whose premise is that everything is a plugin -- reaches the unfenced path by importing it. The unfenced function's JSDoc already says it cannot enforce authority, and documentation is not a gate: a consumer need not read it and the compiler will not object. The characterization case therefore asserts BOTH outcomes on one forged proposal -- refused through the fenced entry, ADMITTED through the public one. That case PASSING is the defect; it starts failing when the unfenced export is withdrawn or gated, which is a P4-05 supersession and not P4-07's to make.

P1-03 P-stage. must[1]'s candidate/verify/atomic-replace, plus acceptance[2]'s concurrency control.

ORDER IS THE MECHANISM and one case pins it: validation runs BEFORE the base comparison, because an invalid candidate is wrong regardless of what else happened and reporting a base mismatch would send its author to fix the wrong thing. The observedBase parameter is what makes concurrent installs safe -- two processes that both read version 3 would otherwise each silently replace the other's work, leaving a profile describing one install while holding the other's plugins.

A LIMIT IS RECORDED RATHER THAN PAPERED OVER. Replacing writeLockAtomically's temp-and-rename with an in-place write reddens ZERO cases, and that is stated in the suite's own module comment, in the README, and here. Atomicity is a property of rename(2), not of this module; observing a partial write would require a reader racing the writer. What the cases DO prove is that the content lands whole and no scratch file survives. The alternative -- asserting that renameSync was called -- would be the 'assert a function was called' shape this program rejects, and would convert an honest gap into a green that means nothing.

TWO MUTATIONS INITIALLY REDDENED ZERO AND BOTH WERE BROKEN EDITS, NOT TEST GAPS. Re-applied correctly, removing the concurrency check and dropping the trailing newline each redden 1. Worth recording because a mutation that leaves the file syntactically invalid reports 'no tests' rather than 'no failures', and reading that as 'the suite is insensitive' would have been a false finding in the opposite direction from the usual one.

PRE-FLIGHT: apps/cli/src/profile-boot.ts IS the real seam -- pre-mount admission already happens in composeProfile, and 'digest' and 'integrity' appear ZERO times in that file, so must[2] has a genuine empty subject rather than a name collision. Contrast the three collisions found in P4-06 and P4-07, where the vocabulary was absent because the file was about something else entirely.

THE CALL SITE IS DELIBERATELY NOT WIRED, and this is the substance of the stage rather than an omission. Nothing in this repository generates a lock, so every existing profile is unlocked, and wiring the gate means choosing what a production boot does with an unlocked profile. 'refuse' is must[2]'s literal reading and breaks every boot; 'warn-and-proceed' breaks nothing and lets must[2] read as enforced while enforcing nothing on every profile in existence. Neither is safe to pick while implementing, so the policy is a REQUIRED PARAMETER with no default -- the repository's own rule that defaulting is an explicit resolve() step, never a hidden ?? default. Filed as BLOCKED-094.

The admitted outcome carries verified: true|false so a caller cannot mistake an unlocked boot for a checked one whichever policy is chosen -- without it, 'loaded successfully' would mean two different things. And the policy governs ONLY the absent-lock case: a profile that HAS a lock is judged against it whatever the policy says, which one mutation exists specifically to protect, since otherwise warn-and-proceed would become a way to skip verification entirely.

It starts failing when a real signature root lands, and that failure is the unlock signal.

Reporting the digest would tell an operator the package was tampered with when the real event is that a different version is installed. effectClass is DECLARED by the script, never inferred from what a step did: inferring it would mean deciding after the fact whether an effect escaped, which is exactly what cannot be known from inside the process that crashed. And `verified` is a separate field from `outcome` because 'it finished' and 'we checked it' are different facts.

PRE-FLIGHT on session.ts, and the verdict needed reading rather than counting. Every P4-08 term scores ZERO there (journal/resume/digest/step/receipt/replay/checkpoint), which by itself is the same signal P4-06 got from dispatch.ts. Same distinction, opposite conclusion, and the counts alone could not tell them apart.

AN ENTRY IS WRITTEN WHEN A STEP STARTS, not when it finishes, and that ordering is the whole reason a journal survives a crash. A process killed mid-step leaves an in-flight entry, which decideResume re-runs. Recording only on completion would leave no trace of the step at all, and a resume would believe it never began -- indistinguishable from a step whose side effect escaped just before the kill. That mutation reddens 11 of 13.

THE RECORDER INVENTS NOTHING. A settlement for a step that never started is DROPPED rather than back-filled: an entry conjured there would carry an effect class nobody declared, and decideResume would then act on a guess. Verification is refused for in-flight and failed steps, with a positive control beside both refusals so a recorder that verified nothing could not satisfy them.

ONE MUTATION FIRST REDDENED ZERO and the suite was the thing at fault, not the mutation: entries are keyed by seq and sorted, but every existing case STARTED its steps in order, so insertion order and sequence order coincided and the sort was never exercised. parallel() begins several agent() calls concurrently, so out-of-order starts are real. A case that starts 3, 1, 2 was added; the mutation now reddens it.

THE ADAPTER DECIDES NOTHING, deliberately. It maps one event shape to another; every judgement -- what may be skipped, what must be reconciled, whether a resume is allowed -- stays in ./types.ts where it is testable without a running worker. `classify` is a CALLER-SUPPLIED parameter for the same reason the effect class is declared rather than inferred: an adapter guessing by label, by phase, or by whether a result came back would be inferring whether an effect escaped from outside the process that produced it.

A cancelled step produced no result, so a resume must re-run it, which is what `failed` already means to decideResume; a third outcome would create a state every consumer must handle and none would treat differently. A positive control sits beside it (`completed` maps differently), since a function returning 'failed' unconditionally would otherwise satisfy the mapping case.

P4-09 C-stage. Per-stage freeze-target list made before any code (C first, written out); path patch for nested.e2e.spec.ts recorded before the first line -- fourth application of BLOCKED-070's prevention subclass. The list again produced answers that would otherwise have surfaced late: P declares ONE source file and no test, U declares two source files and no test AND belongs in workflow-worker-thread rather than this package.

A RUN PINS A DIGEST, NOT A NAME. A name can be repointed at different code, so a run recorded against one cannot be reproduced. The digest covers the BODY ALONE -- including the name or version would give one source two identities, and a run recorded under either could not be recognized as the same work. canResumeAgainst answers by digest and never by version, so a newer version under the same name does not make an old run resumable: that is different code the run never referenced, and upgrading is a deliberate migration rather than something a version comparison authorizes.

THE SUPPLIED DIGEST IS RECOMPUTED, NOT TRUSTED. A caller-supplied digest nobody checks would let a registration claim one identity and store another, after which every resolution would be exact about the wrong thing.

acceptance[0] IS DEMONSTRATED, NOT ASSERTED: a case registers and resolves a definition whose body is `process.exit(1); throw new Error("executed")`. Every function here either hashes a body or pattern-matches it, so a hostile body behaves exactly like any other. declaresNestedCall is textual for the same reason -- parsing would mean building an evaluator, and over-reporting is the safe direction.

RECURSION IS CHECKED BEFORE DEPTH, and a case pins that ordering with a child that would fail both. A depth limit halts a recursive definition eventually, but reports the same failure for one that is merely deeply composed; reporting depth for a self-call would tell an operator to raise a limit when the definition never terminates.

P4-09 P-stage: the registry that holds definitions.

SELF-RECURSION IS REFUSED AT REGISTRATION, not left to admitNestedRun. Catching it at run time would mean the definition had already been stored, shipped, and started before anyone learned it cannot terminate. A positive control sits beside it -- a definition nesting a DIFFERENT workflow registers fine -- since otherwise a registry refusing every body containing the word `workflow` would satisfy the refusal case.

A REFUSED REGISTRATION MUST NOT BE STORED, and a case checks the store afterwards rather than only the return value: a store that retained it would let a run resolve a definition the registry declined.

ONE MUTATION IS A GENUINE EQUIVALENT MUTANT, and it is recorded rather than patched around -- BLOCKED-098's shape appearing a second time, correctly identified this time as equivalent instead of as a gap. Replacing current()'s highest-version reduce with 'last element' reddens NOTHING, and reading establishes why: byName.set is the sole writer to that array and is reached only after admitRegistration has required version === highest + 1, so insertion order always equals version order.

THE EQUIVALENCE IS GUARANTEED BY AN INVARIANT IN ANOTHER MODULE, which is the part worth recording. THE ATOMICITY IS STATED AT ITS REAL STRENGTH, in the module doc and here. Read-decide-write happens with no suspension point between the steps, so two callers within ONE PROCESS cannot interleave and both write themselves as owner. A shared store across processes would need the write to be conditional on the attempt number it read -- a compare-and-set the backing store enforces -- and that is NOT implemented. Recorded because 'atomic' invites more confidence than this implementation earns, the same way 'one batch' did not mean 'one transaction' in P4-06.

THE DECISION IS DELEGATED, NOT REIMPLEMENTED: claim() calls the pure decideClaim rather than repeating its rule, so the store cannot drift from the contract the Contract stage froze.

A TEST OF MINE ASSERTED SOMETHING FALSE AND CHECKING IT TAUGHT ME ABOUT MY OWN DESIGN. The first version claimed a cycle could close across two separately-valid submissions and expected a refusal; it went green the other way, because `a depends on b` with b present IS acyclic. Following that: a cross-batch cycle is UNREACHABLE, since closing one needs an already-stored task to depend on a task submitted later, and such a task is refused at its own submission as an unknown dependency. So the forward-reference rule -- not the combined-graph walk -- is what rules out cross-batch cycles, and the combined walk is belt-and-braces that keeps a dependency on a stored task resolvable. The case now asserts what is actually true, and a second case covers what the combined walk really buys.

P4-07 F-stage. 16 boundaries enumerated as data with the count asserted against validation[0]'s floor of 12, including its two named scenarios: a delayed packet from a reclaimed holder refused on arrival, and split brain across a reclaim where only the later holder writes.

PRE-FLIGHT on validation[2] ('stale token rejection is written to audit'). The subject is HALF present, measured rather than assumed: TrustKernel.auditAppend is literally `(_entry: TrustKernelAuditEntry): void => {}` and the kernel exposes NO read member at all -- by design, since a function type with that signature cannot expose one. So an appended entry is unobservable to anything, a test included. The producible half is real and is built: describeFencingRejection returns a complete record naming who was refused, who was current, and why. It deliberately carries no signature, key, or secret material -- the record describes an authorization DECISION, and quoting the token's credentials would leak them into whatever backs the audit chain. A KNOWN GAP case states plainly which half is proved.

RESIDUAL PINNED AS A MEASURED FACT, per the delegate's ruling, and it is TWO facts kept apart. decideTransition adopting a proposal's epoch is permissive but harmless alone; what makes it REACHABLE is that advanceAgentLifecycle is a PUBLIC EXPORT of dsh-agent, so any consumer -- including a third-party plugin, in a product whose premise is that everything is a plugin -- reaches the unfenced path by importing it. The unfenced function's JSDoc already says it cannot enforce authority, and documentation is not a gate: a consumer need not read it and the compiler will not object. The characterization case therefore asserts BOTH outcomes on one forged proposal -- refused through the fenced entry, ADMITTED through the public one. That case PASSING is the defect; it starts failing when the unfenced export is withdrawn or gated, which is a P4-05 supersession and not P4-07's to make.

Authorized by decision C3, which cleared P9-01..07 to start ahead of W20-W22; the freeze schema's epic pattern was widened from ^P[0-8]- to ^P[0-9]- in the same change, since a schema that rejects P9 makes the approved slice impossible to run. The ladder's tiers are exact, trailing-whitespace and indentation -- NOT the three fixture classes the epic's text names. fsio.ts normalizes line endings on both the content and the search text before matching, so CRLF/LF already resolves at the exact tier; a CRLF tier would be a branch no input can reach, reporting success for work the exact tier had already done. The frozen case asserting CRLF resolves AT THE EXACT TIER is therefore deliberately a different claim from 'a CRLF fallback works'. The other load-bearing case is that an ambiguous tier fails closed rather than falling through: falling through would let a looser tier pick one region out of text a stricter tier already found twice, converting an ambiguity into a confident wrong edit. Scope is deliberately the pure decision only: must[1] requires a typed `budget-exceeded` session event, and a new SessionEventMap member reaches both SDKs' expected outputs and the recorded snapshots, so wiring it into ReactLoopAgent is Usage-stage work and `agent.ts` is untouched here. entries.note: C (Contract) for P9-05, DELIBERATELY HALF THE EPIC. BLOCKED-107 established that must[0] (exact DeepSeek counting) and must[2] (p95 error against four corpora) both need a tokenizer whose source is a maintainer's decision, and that must[1] and must[3] are reachable today. This is must[1] and must[3] only; the other two are untouched and remain blocked. TWO OF MY OWN ASSERTIONS WERE FALSE AND WERE CORRECTED BY RUNNING THEM. (1) I asserted the error narrows strictly every round; on constant-density content the factor reaches the truth in two rounds, so the third comparison demanded better than exact. (2) I asserted a converged estimate is never exact — false for uniform content, where it can be. The real limitation is different and is now the case that states it: on content whose density VARIES the single factor oscillates, tracking whichever content came last, and twenty observations buy nothing the first two did not. That is the honest form of why must[0] needs a tokenizer.

entries.note:
P8-01 must[4] supplement, seq 1. Not a re-freeze: the four primary cells' cases do not touch must[4], and none is edited here.

WHAT must[4] ASKS AND WHAT WAS BUILDABLE. Two halves -- the protocol schema artifact enters GOLDEN COMPATIBILITY FIXTURES, and it enters RELEASE EVIDENCE. The first is built as a generated artifact with a `--check` mode, which is what makes it a fixture rather than a report: a committed file that must match a fresh generation, so acceptance[3] is enforced instead of asserted. The `--check` gate runs in the registry gate set, so a protocol change cannot land without regenerating it.

GENERATED FROM THE SURFACE, NEVER TRANSCRIBED BESIDE IT. The document is built from SERVER_PROTOCOL_SURFACE, the same value initialize fingerprints for a peer. That constant is newly exported for this: a hand-maintained schema file would be a second declaration of the surface, free to disagree with the one peers actually meet, and a golden fixture pinning a disagreeing copy reports drift that is not there while missing drift that is.

THE FINGERPRINT IS PINNED AS A LITERAL, and both directions are asserted -- the committed artifact holds it, AND the live surface produces it. Either alone is satisfiable by a fixture that agrees only with itself: a stale digest in the file passes the first, and a test recomputing the digest from the surface it is checking passes no matter what the surface says.

THE CONTROL IS NOT DECORATION. Reordering the surface must NOT move the fingerprint. Without that case, a fingerprint that moved on any edit at all -- including ones no peer can observe -- would satisfy the acceptance[3] case, and a fixture that cries wolf stops being consulted. The mutation proof confirms it discriminates: the CONTROL reddens under a real wire-visible change and holds under a reorder.

RELEASE EVIDENCE USES THE REAL COLLECTOR, P0-07's scripts/release/collect-evidence.mjs, against a throwaway checkout carrying a real copy of the artifact -- `init` binds a captured baseline whose gitSha must equal HEAD, so running it against this repository would either fail or write into it. The case asserts the recorded digest equals the artifact's real bytes AND that the package accepts only because the declared artifact is present; a second case proves the digest tracks the file, which a collector recording a constant or hashing the path would fail.

BLOCKED WHY, AND FOR HOW LONG. This wiring was blocked from 2026-09-05 to 2026-09-06 by BLOCKED-077, recorded as an unexplained stack overflow. The cause was a stale `packages/action/action-manifest/src/canonicalize.js` holding the SUPERSEDED recursive implementation beside the iterative `.ts`; the module resolver ran the artifact. A round of investigation had already excluded that function by reading `src/` and the built `lib/` -- both iterative, both correct, and neither the code that ran.

A SECOND FALSE TRAIL, recorded because it cost an afternoon. With the overflow fixed, appending the manifest still timed out ten of this file's cases, and the cause was this file's own `fakeAgent`: a structural fake carrying `append` and `header`, cast through `as unknown as Agent`. Reaching any third member throws inside the scheduler lane, the dispatch never settles, and unrelated cases time out -- which reads as a concurrency defect. Isolating it to a single statement is what found it; two hypotheses about production code were formed first and both were wrong. A double narrower than the interface it stands for does not fail where the member is missing.

THE ABANDONED-DISPATCH CASE IS WHY THE PLACEMENT IS AT `start`. A queued call the run settlement abandons never executes, and a manifest for it would record an action that did not happen -- the opposite failure from the one acceptance[0] names, and just as wrong. Appending at binding entry would have produced exactly that.

P2-03 F-stage. First freeze for this cell.

SCOPE. validation[2] -- fuzz the canonicalizer, forbidding key order / Unicode / number spelling from confusing the hash. The Contract stage pinned those three confusions with ONE example each; three examples cannot say whether a property holds, and the clause asks for fuzzing precisely because a canonicalizer fails on the input nobody thought to write.

BOTH DIRECTIONS, because either alone is satisfiable by a broken implementation. Same value in a different spelling must collide, or a replay of an identical action is refused as tampering. Different values must NOT collide, or a substituted argument passes as the one that was authorised. A canonicalizer returning a constant satisfies the first; one hashing raw bytes satisfies the second.

A GENERATOR THAT STARVES IS NOT A PASSING PROPERTY. The Unicode case is built from characters that decompose rather than filtered from arbitrary strings. Filtering looked correct and hung the suite: `fc.string()` almost never produces a value whose NFD differs from its NFC, so the run spent its whole budget rejecting inputs. It never reported that it had tested nothing.

ONE CASE CLAIMED MORE THAN IT TESTS, and the mutation is what found it -- see sensitivityProof. Recorded here because a reader of this cell should know which of its four cases is load-bearing for validation[2] and which is a difference check whose original justification was wrong.

validation[1] (replay pairing manifest -> decision -> execution -> result) is NOT covered by this cell. `decision` means the policy/approval step, and no such step exists on this path yet -- P2-05 owns the Policy Decision Service. Asserting the pairing today would assert a three-link chain against two links present, which is BLOCKED-050's shape.

EFFECTIVE SAMPLES, measured rather than assumed: key-order 500/500, Unicode 200/200, no-collision 500/500, separator 300/300 — every property runs its whole budget with ZERO precondition rejections. Recorded because that is the number a starving generator destroys while the suite stays green: the first Unicode generator filtered arbitrary strings and would have shown a tiny fraction here, and it reported nothing on its own. A later change to any generator should be checked against these counts, not against the suite's colour.

sensitivityProof.mutationDescription: Two mutations of packages/action/action-manifest/src/canonicalize.ts, each restored byte-identical: (M1) object keys sort by `localeCompare` instead of by code unit; (M2) keys are not sorted at all. Plus a REVERSE mutation of the tests: both SECURITY cases assert that NFC and NFD share a hash, which is the requirement this correction removed. A third mutation removes `assertJsonArguments` from `createActionManifest`.
sensitivityProof.failureSummary: M1 reddens EXACTLY ONE case -- the differential property against the reference implementation -- and nothing else. That result is what justifies the oracle: `localeCompare` still sorts, so every named property (key order, number spelling, escape spelling, NFC-versus-NFD) still holds, and only agreement with RFC 8785 itself detects the difference. M2 reddens three, including the differential one. The reverse mutation reddens both SECURITY cases and nothing else, which is what says they assert the corrected direction rather than merely reacting to any change in the canonicalizer. Removing the manifest-layer refusal reddens exactly the non-finite SECURITY case and nothing else, which is what says the refusal lives at the manifest and not in the canonicalizer -- the canonicalizer's own agreement with the reference is untouched by it.

entries.note:
P2-03 C-stage, SUPERSEDING the 2026-09-05 freeze. Supersession rather than supplement because four of its cases asserted behaviour this correction PROHIBITS -- a supplement adds coverage without disturbing what is there, and what was there is what had to change.

WHAT CHANGED AND WHY. `canonicalizeArguments` normalized strings and keys to NFC. RFC 8785 deliberately does not: two code point sequences are two values. Normalizing meant a precomposed and a decomposed spelling of one character produced a single `argumentsHash`, and P2-06 binds approvals to that hash -- so where those spellings name two different files, approving one action authorised the other. The clause forbade hash confusion and the implementation committed it, in the direction the clause had not considered. It also broke cross-language agreement by construction, since P8-07's Python side uses a standard JCS library that does not normalize either.

THE OLD CASE ASSERTED THE DEFECT, AND CARRIED A MUTATION PROOF. The case reading 'strings in different Unicode normalization forms hash identically' was frozen with evidence that the suite was sensitive to it. A mutation proof shows a suite notices what it asserts; it says NOTHING about whether the assertion is right. What decides that is the clause wording, the make-vs-use ledger's risk note for this epic, and the security consequence -- and all three pointed the other way while that case sat green.

WHY THE IMPLEMENTATION IS STILL HAND-WRITTEN, and how that stays honest. Every JavaScript RFC 8785 library recurses: measured 2026-09-06, `canonicalize` 2.1.0 handles depth 1000 and overflows at 5000, and 4.0.0 and `json-canonicalize` 3.0.0 overflow at 5000 as well. The code-mode dispatch path produces arguments that deep -- ptc.spec.ts dispatches at exactly 5000 -- so no available library can do what this call site requires. The exception is not habit, and it is not defended by a comment: `canonicalize@2.1.0` is a devDependency used as a differential ORACLE, and a property case asserts byte-identical agreement with it over 1000 generated values spanning both normalization forms, escapes, surrogate pairs, negative zero, 1e21, 1e-7 and integers past 2^53. Agreeing with a list of four named properties is weaker than agreeing with the reference, and M1 is the proof: a wrong sort passes every named property and fails only the oracle.

THE DECOMPOSED FORM IS BUILT FROM CODE POINTS, NEVER WRITTEN AS A LITERAL. A shell or an editor may normalize a source file, and the case would then compare a string with itself and pass while testing nothing. That happened once while verifying the replacement library, and the first measurement it produced was wrong in the reassuring direction.

THE VALUE DOMAIN IS THE MANIFEST'S CONTRACT, NOT THE CANONICALIZER'S. `{amount: Infinity}` canonicalizes to `{"amount":null}` -- correct per RFC 8785, which builds on JSON -- so it shares an argumentsHash with an action whose amount really is null, and P2-06 binds approvals to that hash. That is the same confusion the NFC normalization caused, reached from the value domain instead of the encoding. `createActionManifest` refuses non-finite numbers and bigints, naming the offending path; a real null stays legal, which is what makes the refusal mean something rather than banning the shape. Putting the refusal in the canonicalizer would have put it out of step with the reference implementation, and the differential case would have caught that immediately.

entries.note:
P2-03 F-stage, SUPERSEDING the 2026-09-06 morning freeze -- eight hours old, and superseded because its Unicode fuzz case asserted the defect.

The case now asserts the opposite: NFD and NFC never share a hash, over generated strings that have two forms. Its generator is unchanged and still builds from characters that decompose rather than filtering arbitrary strings, because a filter starved and hung the suite without reporting that it had tested nothing.

RECORDED BECAUSE IT IS THE POINT: this cell was frozen WITH a mutation proof, and that proof was correct. The suite was sensitive to the property it asserted. The property was wrong. Sensitivity and correctness are different questions, and only the first is mechanical.

entries.note: SLICE-fiber-A supersession, delegate-approved 2026-09-06 (ruling 2). The three superseded cases froze the KNOWN RESIDUAL -- they asserted that poisoning a non-root fiber's store DID forge ctx.trustKernel. The slice closes that residual, so the cases now assert a defect that no longer exists; under BLOCKED-066 that is a supersession, not a refinement, because the property being asserted changed rather than being stated more precisely. The three replacements assert the refusals: the attacker's own-fiber write is refused and resolves to the real kernel; an ancestor-fiber write is refused and reaches no plugin nested under it; and a wholesale store-object replacement is RE-SEALED rather than refused, because the guard lives in the setter. RED->GREEN measured in both directions: with the vendored patch reverted, exactly these three fail and the three protection cases still pass; with it applied, 53/53 in packages/kernel/trust-kernel. P0-02 stays ACCEPTED -- its acceptance bound the candidate observed at the time, and this changes what is frozen going forward, not what was verified then. Implementation: vendor/README.md local modification 20; re-vendor condition BLOCKED-130; boundary doc's known-residual section marked closed with the heading kept so its six inbound links still resolve.

sensitivityProof.failureSummary: Without the fix: 3 failed | 3 passed (6). The three failures are exactly the three new cases -- "refuses a write to the attacking plugin's own fiber store...", "refuses the ancestor-store write...", and "re-seals the pinned name when the store field is reassigned..." -- while the three pre-existing protection cases (impl.value, root-store key write, reflect.props) still passed, so the mutation is discriminating rather than breaking the file wholesale. With the fix restored: 6 passed (6), and 53/53 across packages/kernel/trust-kernel. This is a RED->GREEN proof in both directions on the superseding cases themselves. Recorded caveat, per the rule this program has already written down twice: a mutation proof shows the suite is SENSITIVE to what it asserts and says nothing about whether the assertion is correct -- the correctness argument here is the probe that first measured the forgery succeeding (propertyForged: true on a non-root fiber) before any fix existed.
