entries.supersessionReason: §12.47(ii). The C stage over-read must[3]: the clause says an unknown action defaults to a HIGHER class, and P2-03's acceptance[2] says an unclassifiable one defaults to high risk AND REQUIRES APPROVAL — both name approval, not refusal. Freezing `UNKNOWN_DEFAULT_CLASS` at `safety-critical`, which is the kernel hard-deny band, equated "we do not know what this is" with "we know this is catastrophic", and since nothing declares domain tags yet, wiring the gate on top of it would have refused every action outright rather than asked about any. This is a property change, not a wording change, so it supersedes rather than renames: the unknown default is now the highest POLICY-ADJUSTABLE class and `safety-critical` is reached by declaration. The C cell was NOT_RUN, so no observation binds to the superseded entry.

entries.note: P1-03 Usage supplement 1: must[2]'s PRODUCT half. A SUPPLEMENT and not a supersession, decided by reading the primary entry rather than by the lock row's wording -- the row says 'as a supersession', but it was written before BLOCKED-103 set the rule. The primary U entry's five cases all test `gateProductionBoot`'s DECISION logic in isolation (gate.spec.ts), every one is still true, none asserts that decision-level coverage is sufficient, and none is contradicted by comparing real recorded integrity. Re-run at this tree: 5/5 passing. So they are kept and these nine are added beside them, the P2-03 code-mode shape. What these nine reach that the primary five could not: the gate had zero call sites outside its own package, so 'the gate refuses a drifted digest' and 'a boot was refused' were different claims. These drive `composeProfile`'s two entry points against a real profile directory and the real plugins.lock.json the `dsh plugin` transaction writes. Two of the nine are controls and are load-bearing as such: without #2 the drift refusal is satisfied by a gate that refuses everything, and without #7 most-restrictive-wins is satisfied by a function returning 'refuse' always. NOT claimed: acceptance[0]'s product half. The lock row says acceptance[0] is proven at the decision level rather than by a real cold start, and that stays true -- a cold start means booting with no network available, which none of these cases does. It becomes a second lock row owned by P1-03's F stage (delegate ruling, 2026-09-06). Writing it into coverage would be the assertion-with-no-subject shape. The `supplements` back-reference was missing when this entry was first written, so the greening path could not find it — added here; the entry's argv, files, cases and proofs are unchanged.

entries.note: acceptance[0]'s two halves, frozen as F supplement 1 under the delegate's ruling (A) — reusing apps/cli/tests/plugin-lock.spec.ts and listing only this stage's own additions, the P8-01 precedent for a shared spec file. STRUCTURAL half: the delegate first specified a `fetch` spy asserting zero calls. Measured before building, profile-boot has no fetch, no node:http(s), no net., and its whole closure is 7 workspace packages plus js-yaml and resolve.exports — so `calls === 0` is true of EVERY implementation, including one with no cache lookup at all, and the proposed reverse control could never fire. The delegate withdrew it. What replaces it can fail: the gate refuses an HTTP client in any manifest or an egress in any source of the closure, and four of its five cases exist to prove it goes red. BEHAVIOURAL half: `admitBoot`'s `missing-from-disk` branch, checked to exist before the case was written. NOT claimed: that a missing cache entry is refused rather than FETCHED. No such branch exists because no network path exists. acceptance[0] holds because there is nothing to omit, not because a fallback was exercised, and those are different evidence.

entries.note: P2-02 must[1]'s signing half. What it replaces: `issueToken`/`attenuateToken` wrote a fixed four-byte marker and `verifyToken` compared a candidate against that same constant — identical in EVERY installation, so another deployment's token verified here and verification could not fail. The parameters were literally named `_trustRoot`: the handle was taken and ignored. This is the third occurrence of one shape in this program (the plugin lock's `unavailable:` integrity, the boot-path fetch assertion, this marker), and the tell each time is a comparison whose two sides come from the same place. The third case PASSED before the key existed and is a regression guard rather than a driver: `signatureRoots` was `Object.freeze({})`, so 'the private key is not on the handle' was trivially true. It is frozen because the handle crosses the plugin boundary and is exactly where a refactor would put the key by accident. Scope, per the delegate's ruling: must[1] is issuance/verification/attenuation and does NOT include key LIFETIME. Persistence, rotation, the 0600 dev file backend, `production-controlled` refusing a file backend, and the survives-a-restart case are SLICE-kernel-keys, due before P4-04. This makes a token's issuer checkable against a root the deployment configured; whether that root is the right one is P1-02's question, under P1-02's own lock. A workflow run is the work item because it is the thing two hosts could both believe they own: durable id, state its parent reads, outliving individual messages. The work item is the SESSION, not the Run. `run-<uuid>` is minted on every open, so two hosts driving one session asked for two different items and neither `acquire` could refuse the other — measured with two processes over one SQLite lease store, both producing a granted lease at epoch 0. acceptance[1]'s 'does not produce two masters' therefore held vacuously: the thing two hosts actually open at once is a durable session. This also makes §12.31-A's `lease-refused` reachable in production for the first time: until now the only refusal a real deployment could produce was an unavailable store. entries.note: §12.35-2. The bypass one layer below the manifest: P2-03's must[2] was closed for the manifest and left open for the ledger, so an external effect performed from a code-mode program took no reservation at all. `reserveExternalEffect`, `confirmExternalEffect` and the refusal text moved from the agent loop into `@deepseek-ai/dsh-tools/external-effect`, which both dispatch paths can reach; writing them a second time in `ptc.ts` is BLOCKED-136's shape. The context comes from the registry through a closure rather than from `exec.agent.ctx`: a sub-dispatch's agent handle need not have one, and reading it threw inside `commit` where the rejection surfaced as four cases hanging to their timeout rather than as an error — the failure mode this file's own comments already warned about. On identity (§12.36): the sub-call id is `<run_code callId>:code:<ordinal>`, so two identical calls INSIDE one program are two actions and both run, while a replay of the same `run_code` call reproduces the same ids and the same keys and the second is refused. That is the code-mode analogue of the native path replaying a model call id, and it corrects an earlier report of mine that concluded the key could never collide. A refusal reaches the program as a THROW rather than a return: a refused sub-call produced no result, and handing one back would let a program read 'already performed' as a fresh success.

entries.note: §12.37. The inbox's dequeue ordering was never frozen: §12.25-1 put the shared table at the claim boundary and froze nothing there, which is why reversing it broke two cases in `@deepseek-ai/dsh-experimental-agent-team` — a consumer of the inbox, in the full suite and not in the packages I ran — and CI found it rather than a freeze. This entry is that missing freeze, taken at the corrected rule. must[1]'s per-kind priority governs conflicts between control DECISIONS, not the order of content inside a batch: an `inject` is context, and moving a later-arriving instruction ahead of context that preceded it changes what that instruction means. Only `cancel` is promoted; `human-answer` is positioned by the wait point it answers; everything else, including ordinary input carrying no kind, keeps arrival order, supplied by the comparator's explicit index tiebreak rather than by sort stability. The two earlier cases stated the overturned rule in their own TITLES ('orders a MIXED-SOURCE batch by kind, not by arrival'), so they were renamed rather than re-asserted: a title that names a reversed rule would freeze it again.

entries.note: §12.35-2(c), §12.39, §12.42. The send side had no producer: `dispatchOnce`'s only caller in the repository was an experimental package that does not ship, and the one real handoff between agents — a child telling its parent how it ended — was hand-delivered, so a parent that was gone, tearing down, or unreachable got a log line and nothing else. Pre-step alone would deadlock — an idle parent waiting on its child has no step to take. entries.filesOverlayReason: §12.47(i). The registry's P file list names only `risk-taxonomy/src/index.ts`, which would make the Provider stage a barrel edit and leave the seam without a Provider: `classify` takes the organisation policy as a PARAMETER, so nothing classifies anything until a mount binds it. The plan listed one file because it had not applied the capability-seam rule, not because the Provider role was meant to be absent.

That is a property change rather than a wording change — the field moved, the resolution rule is new, and a fallback for a preset the table does not carry did not exist before — so it supersedes rather than renames. THE GAP THIS STAGE CLOSES WAS MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED. advanceAgentLifecycle cannot enforce authority, and the reason is structural: NOTHING ISSUES THE LIFECYCLE'S EPOCH. decideTransition refuses only a strictly OLDER epoch and then adopts whatever the proposal carried, so the epoch a lifecycle holds is only ever the last one a caller asserted. A worker proposing epoch 9999 against a lifecycle at 1 is admitted AND becomes the new authority. A CHARACTERIZATION case pins that behaviour directly, so the fenced entry point is measured against a real hole rather than an imagined one.

P4-05'S CONTRACT WAS NOT EDITED. The gap is closed from outside: checkFencing runs against the store's current lease first, so the epoch reaching decideTransition is one the STORE issued rather than one the caller chose. The two staleness rules stay deliberately different and this is not a contradiction -- decideTransition compares against a lifecycle that LEARNS its epoch from transitions, so it must admit a newer one; checkFencing compares against a store that ISSUES epochs, so anything but the current one is a forgery. Running the issuer's check first makes the lifecycle's more permissive rule unreachable by an attacker.

ORDER IS PART OF THE CONTRACT, and one case exists only to pin it. A token that is BOTH fenced and proposing an illegal edge must report 'fenced'. This applies the principle already stated in decideTransition's own JSDoc -- ordering authority first means 'a stale worker never learns whether its proposed edge would have been legal'. Running fencing after the lifecycle decision leaks exactly that to a worker with no authority to ask. The first draft of this suite had no such case and the reordering mutation reddened ZERO; the case was added rather than the mutation dismissed as equivalent.

P4-05's lifecycle types were internal to dsh-agent and are now exported, because P4-07's fenced entry point takes them as parameters and an outside caller could not otherwise name what it must pass. Same shape as P8-01's Provider stage, where a missing re-export WAS the stage's substance. The subject is HALF present, measured rather than assumed: TrustKernel.auditAppend is literally `(_entry: TrustKernelAuditEntry): void => {}` and the kernel exposes NO read member at all -- by design, since a function type with that signature cannot expose one. entries.note: §12.67 item 4. SUPERSEDED, not renamed — the property changed. §12.46-A removed the `pure` gate from compaction because it could never fire: `replay.ts` gated on `completed && verified && pure`, and a step is classed side-effecting whenever it may have left the harness, so the pure conjunct excluded every step the gate was written for. The guard is now VERIFICATION, and the ledger reconciles the effect. So a completed, verified step is compacted WHATEVER its effect class, and what stays untouched is an UNVERIFIED step rather than a side-effecting one. The old titles assert the opposite guard and cannot be satisfied by the current code, which is why registering them as renames would record a continuity that does not hold (the §12.61 reading applied to P4-12.C.1). Boundary 15 still exists and still guards, on a different predicate; boundary 16 (compaction retains every receipt) is new, so the matrix grew rather than shrank and its 'at least twelve boundaries' assertion is unaffected.

entries.note: P2-02 base U, SUPERSEDING the pre-withdrawal base U (#69). §12.53: two live base U entries would leave 4.4b and predicate (iii) reading two different truths about one stage. #69's 18 titles are ABSORBED rather than dropped — they remain true and they remain necessary, but they are DECISION-level: every one of them passed in the world the withdrawal was about, because they verify `delegatedChildResources`, the widening refusals, the depth and digest on tokens the case itself constructs, while nothing in the harness derived a token at all. The 9 provider cases add REACH (a mount issues, arms, re-issues on growth, revokes per session, and writes no key), and the 4 spawn cases add the delegation the epic's title names, read off a child the spawn provider actually started rather than a pair built in the test. The spawn cases are CONTINUABLE deliberately: a one-shot child has already completed and disposed by the time `start` resolves and `agent/disposed` drops its token, so a one-shot harness observes `undefined` and reads as 'delegation does not happen' when what it measured was a dead session. The fifth spawn case pins that a cancelled TURN does not revoke delegated authority: `Agent.cancel` is turn-scoped and P5-10's semantics are that cancelling is not disconnecting, so a continuable child outliving one cancelled turn is the delegated lifetime working. It was MEASURED before anything was wired (§12.77, `evidence-P2-02.md`), because the alternative — wiring `revokeSession(parent)` at the cancel path — would have revoked the parent's own root and refused its next turn.

entries.note: P2-04 base U (§12.72), superseding the two supplements that were this stage's only entries. Neither #208 nor #210 was a base, so predicate (iii) saw two partial observations of one stage and 4.4b had no single command to read — the same two-live-entries shape §12.53 closes for P2-02. The ten titles are the union, unchanged: three for must[1]'s declaration reaching the runtime and never the model, seven for the gate's own decisions — the sandboxed default that does not ask, the undeclared tool that does, the high band that asks and the kernel band that never does, and the composition with no policy service where absence of a capability is not absence of a gate. The eleventh case closes BLOCKED-159 under §12.78: `manifest.requiresApproval` is the action's INTRINSIC classification, recorded before execution and preset-blind, while the gate decides under the preset in force — two different questions, both legitimate. What was not legitimate was the gate's answer leaving no trace, so `action/risk-gated` records every branch. The allow branch is the one the case asserts, because a refusal or an ask leaves other evidence and an allow leaves none: that is the only branch where the audit log and the execution can diverge in silence.

P4-09 U supplement: the token slice, the detached slice and the persistent-descriptor slice, none of which any earlier supplement's argv reached -- U.2 and U.3 freeze the nesting cases that predate them.

THE ENGINE STOPPED REGISTERING AT ALL, and the failures said nothing about why. Declaring `agents` in `static inject` makes Cordis refuse to register the service in every composition that mounts no agent registry, including the seam's own suites: 53 failures reporting `unknown tool "workflow"` and `reading 'start' of undefined`, not one of them naming `inject`. `ctx.get('agents')` with an explicit refusal replaces it, so a composition without an agent registry says so at the call rather than by silently lacking the engine.

A DETACHED RUN NEEDS ITS OWN AGENT, not just its own session id. `deriveChild` takes session IDs, so the token half is satisfiable without one -- I claimed exactly that from reading the code, and it is false of the COMPOSITION: an Agent is the scope its children are created in, so a child composed on the launcher's context dies with it (`cannot create effect on inactive context`) whatever token it holds. M36 is that claim as a mutation.

THE ROUND-TRIP CASE GUARDS TWO LISTS, not one field. `CONTINUABLE_DESCRIPTOR_KEYS` decides which fields are LEGAL to persist; `parseSubagentDescriptor` rebuilds field by field and thereby decides which SURVIVE a read. A field on the first and absent from the second is written, accepted, and read back as `undefined` with no error at either end -- which is what happened to `delegatingSession` on every cold resume while four other links were correctly wired. Reading the code did not find it; a probe above the derivation did. The case drives its payload from the exported field list so a later field cannot be covered by omission, and asserts every declared field has a sample before comparing.

entries.note:
P4-11 Usage stage: must[1] and must[2] acquire callers.

MUST[1] IS ONE LAYER PLUS AN ATTRIBUTION RULE, and the second layer was measured away rather than assumed. §12.64 had ruled that the MCP client would charge retries and reconnects made FOR a run action; measured, every `retry`/`attempt` in `packages/mcp/mcp-client/src` is the connection supervisor's and `connection.ts` references no agent, execution or run at all. A reconnect restores a shared server process -- one supervisor serves every run using it -- so charging the momentarily-active run makes it pay for another's outage. The MCP tool-call path is the opposite: it resolves a run through `exec.agent` and performs no retry. So the layers are `llm-retry` for the parent AND every child session, charged to one run; the subagent is not a second layer but the multiplier of the first, which is what `chargedRun` stops. §12.64's original wording is kept in the preFlight, marked overturned.

THE CARRIER PREMISE WAS ALSO CORRECTED. My first measurement searched for `ctx.runs` consumers OUTSIDE `run/run`, found zero, and read it as 'nothing creates a Run'. `RunPlugin` is its own consumer: it opens a Run from `agent/session-start`, adopts live agents at startup, and is mounted in `bundle/base`. Searching for external consumers of a service that drives itself from events finds nothing and means nothing. What IS zero is narrower and still true: `attachSession` has no production caller, so a Run is 1:1 with a session -- which is exactly why the budget cannot be 'this agent's run'.

MUST[2] GUARDS THE FIRST CHUNK, deliberately. A stream that produced a chunk is evidence the endpoint answered, so the first pull is where endpoint health is observable; a mid-stream failure is the transport's or the model's. Wrapping the whole stream would mean deciding inside the breaker which mid-stream failures are the endpoint's fault, which is the classifier's job and is not observable at a chunk boundary. Stated in both READMEs.

WIRING IT REDDENED THREE EXISTING CASES, each a real defect in the wiring: reading the first `IteratorResult`'s getters outside the `try` let a hostile getter escape instead of becoming a terminal chunk, and yielding the first chunk outside the `try/finally` let a consumer that breaks after one chunk skip adapter cleanup. Both fixed by doing what the loop below already did.

entries.note:
P4-11 Fault stage. Twenty-four boundaries as data with both counts guarded, split where their subjects live: pure decisions in the retry package, endpoint-health rows beside the breaker's shipped consumer, and the vanished-parent row beside the budget it protects.

TWO PROPOSED BOUNDARIES DO NOT EXIST, and the matrix says so rather than simulating them. The budget store has no `readFile`, no `writeFile` and no path -- it is a `Map`, deliberately, because a budget bounds one run's LIVE attempts. And `admit` is a synchronous method exposing no read/write pair a caller could await between, so no interleaving is possible inside one call; a concurrency case would assert what the language guarantees. The concern is kept as boundary 20, which asserts the CONTRACT that makes the race impossible, because a refactor to `usageOf` + `record` is what would reintroduce it.

THE STAGE FOUND A REAL DEFECT IN WHAT THE USAGE STAGE LANDED. `chargedRun` re-walked the delegation chain on every retry, reading LIVE registry state: once a parent agent was disposed the walk stopped at the child, which charged its own run and got a fresh allowance -- the stacking must[1] exists to stop, arriving through the back door, and a continuable child outliving its parent's turn is ordinary (P2-02 measured it). `chargedRunFor` resolves once and remembers; a session's delegation root is fixed at creation, so the first resolution is the only one there is.

TWO CASES IN THIS EPIC WERE VACUOUS UNTIL A MUTATION FAILED TO REDDEN THEM, and both are recorded because the pattern is the lesson: a case whose two readings produce the same number asserts nothing. The parent/child budget case gave 3 requests under either reading until it was rebuilt so they differ (5 against 8); the timeout row tested a 503 twice because of a constructor default.

entries.note:
P1-10 Contract stage. The package did not exist; the subject is new, and it starts as vocabulary plus pure judgements with no I/O and no service, because must[1]'s six phases (freeze, snapshot, migrate in quarantine, validate, atomic switch, health check) are an ordering over real EFFECTS -- a module that could perform one of them would be a second place the upgrade happens.

MUST[2] IS SPLIT, AND THE SPLIT IS MEASURED RATHER THAN STAGED. `requiresApprovalAndExport` decides that an approval and an export are OWED; nothing asks. The epic preFlight had read that the subject already existed in `approval`, and that is half true: `ApprovalRequest` carries a `toolName` (user-approval/src/types.ts:63) and `request()` THROWS outside an open turn (index.ts:207-213), while a plugin upgrade is a CLI command with neither. The refusal is not an oversight to route around -- it protects the `approval/asked` + `approval/decided` audit pair that a reload would otherwise find as crash-tail garbage. Which seam asks is an open ruling and it decides whether must[2] closes in this epic; the code, the tests and both READMEs say so, so green cells here cannot be read as an approval that happens.

REVERSIBILITY IS DECLARED, NOT DERIVED. A snapshot makes the DATA restorable; reversibility asks whether the migration's effects are confined to that data. A migration that also rewrote an external system is irreversible however good its snapshot is, and must[2] exists for exactly that case. M48 is that distinction as a mutation.

A WORKSPACE PATH IS REFUSED, not unsupported (P3-11's boundary), and the comparison carries the separator: without it `<root>-backup` passes as being inside `<root>`, which would let a plugin declare its neighbour's storage as its own backup target.

MUST[2] CLOSES IN THIS EPIC, by the delegate's fourth ruling, and the earlier note above records the measurement that forced the question. For a CLI-driven upgrade, human approval is an operator's explicit confirmation: a TTY prompt, or `--confirm-irreversible <path digest>` without one. A non-interactive run with no flag is refused with NOTHING changed. The confirmation names a digest of the ORDERED steps so it admits one specific conversion; a manifest edited between the operator reading it and the upgrade running produces a different digest and the confirmation stops matching. The export is required BEFORE the confirmation is accepted, because an operator confirming an irreversible conversion is confirming they can still get their data out. Prompting, exporting and recording the confirmation in an append-only transaction log are the Provider stage's; a migration triggered from INSIDE a session belongs to `user-approval` and is P1-11's.

P1-10 Provider stage: the six phases as an ordering over real effects.

THE CASES ASSERT INTERMEDIATE STATES, not an outcome. A transaction whose only evidence is that it returned true is indistinguishable from a function that returns true, so each case reads the disk between phases: production is byte-unchanged while the migration runs against a copy (read DURING the migrate callback, not after), the previous directory survives the switch as a readable rollback target, and a failed health check leaves production byte-identical to the pre-switch rows rather than merely returning an error.

THE SWITCH IS TWO RENAMES on one filesystem, live moved ASIDE first: a rename over a directory does not preserve what it replaced, and the aside IS the rollback target until the health check passes. A failed check renames back and keeps the migrated data in quarantine, because an operator diagnosing the failure needs to see what the migration produced.

TWO PREMISES WERE CORRECTED BEFORE ANY CODE. `write-file-atomic` is an npm package this tree does not have; the house pattern P1-03 established is the repo's own `@deepseek-ai/dsh-atomic-write`, already used by four packages, and adding the npm package would have been a second spelling of a mechanism the tree has. `node:sqlite`'s `VACUUM INTO` was probed on the live runtime rather than assumed — an 8192-byte copy from an in-memory database — so the ledger's `adapt` is executable here.

THE DESTINATION IS BOUND AS A PARAMETER, never interpolated: a storage root can carry a quote, and a path spliced into SQL is an injection even when this file is the only author. A case covers a quoted path.

THE CRASH IS A REAL PROCESS DEATH. P4-09 must[2], the consumer half: a product path that STARTS a detached run.

The provider half was closed earlier: `startDetached` mints the run's own session and agent, `attach(runId)` reaches a run by id, and the run is registered before `workflow/start` fires. What no file did was CALL either from a product path — `tool-workflow` only ever called `start()`, so no turn could start a detached run and no turn could collect one. Under the program's rule (built = a production call site a grep can find), the clause's consumer half had not arrived.

The tool now takes `detached?: boolean` and `attach?: string`. `script`/`meta` stop being schema-required, because an attach call carries neither; the pair is required by the tool instead, which is a relation between arguments a per-field schema cannot state. The detached branch deliberately does NOT pass `exec.signal`: that signal aborts when the step ends, and a run cancelled by the end of the turn that started it is precisely what detached is not.

Observed through the EXECUTOR on the real in-process stack (real worker thread, real spawn backend, one scripted mock model), not through a fake engine: turn one starts detached and aborts its signal, turn two attaches by id alone and receives the value. That case found a real defect — `startDetached` created a bare agent with no LLM route, so the detached script's children failed; the run now inherits the launcher's route exactly as a delegated child does.

entries.note:
P1-10 Usage stage: `dsh plugin add`/`update` runs the transaction, and every phase can refuse.

WHAT REACHES THE PRODUCT: `runPlugin` holds ONE cross-process fencing lease across crash recovery, pnpm, the data migration and layer reconciliation. A lease released between the package manager and the migration reopens exactly the window this epic closes -- new code installed, data not yet converted, another process free to start.

WHAT EACH PHASE NOW DECIDES: `validate` reads the migrated copy back through the facet (it materialized, it carries the version it was migrated TO, the plugin's own optional `validate` export accepts its content); the recorded digest is `digestUnit`'s digest of the CONTENT, so acceptance[1]'s reconciliation compares data with data rather than a version number with another spelling of itself; `healthCheck` opens the unit through the storage hub with the new build's descriptor and reads it, which is the strongest form of 'does the new version work' available to a command that mounts no plugin.

WHAT THE MANIFEST NOW REQUIRES: a step that ships a `module` must declare `reversible` and `backup`, in both the TypeScript validator and the JSON Schema (`dependentRequired`). Nothing is defaulted at the bridge, because a defaulted `reversible: true` made must[2] unreachable in the exact case it exists for.

EVERY REFUSAL IS NAMED, and a refusal is a FAILED upgrade: the code goes back to the version its data is at rather than leaving new code to meet old data at the next boot.

THE CLAUSE THIS STAGE OWNS is must[2]'s 'plugins may only add constraints, never widen'. It is structural rather than tested-into: `PolicyConstraint` is `(request) => string | undefined`, so there is no value a plugin can return that carries a permit. Order-independence follows from that, and the case asserting it names the counter-example — `dsh-permission-rules` resolves ordered allow/deny rules by FIRST MATCH, so under that shape the outcome depends on which of two independently installed plugins loaded first.

THE FIVE INPUTS are all required, including `world` in its `absent` form. `ExecutionWorld` is P3-01's and does not exist; the slot is declared so a request carries the shape must[0] names and so P3-01 landing is a type change rather than a vocabulary change (BLOCKED-178, §12.46-B: rule half here, producer half there). Context facts are a closed enumeration mirroring `workspace-trust`'s own `TrustState` plus the permission posture, rather than a fact bag that would make adding a fact a silent policy change.

THE CEDAR CASES ARE IN THIS STAGE ON PURPOSE. The make-vs-use record's argument for adopting an engine is that forbid-overrides-permit, default-deny and a matched-policy explain are Cedar's semantics; the preFlight recorded them `differs` (unprobed) rather than carrying them from the sheet. `tests/cedar-conformance.spec.ts` runs them against @cedar-policy/cedar-wasm 4.12.0, which moves that row to `ok`. One fact those cases pinned that a provider must not get wrong: submitted as a source STRING, Cedar assigns generated ids (`policy0`, `policy1`) and an `@id(...)` annotation does NOT become the id the explain reports. entries.note:
P1-10's Fault stage: the boundaries where the upgrade's world fails under it, split by whose subject each one is.

WHY TWO FILES AND ONE ARGV. The transaction's boundaries are decided by a fake facet and a fake lease, and live in the package. The consumer's — the module a plugin ships, the recovery pass that runs before the package manager — have their subject in `apps/cli/src/plugin-migration.ts`, and a package test cannot import an app. One argv covers both, because they are one matrix.

THE DECLARED DELIVERABLE COULD NOT HAVE BEEN OBSERVED. The registry names `packages/plugin/plugin-migrations/tests/rollback.e2e.ts`; `.e2e.ts` routes into `vitest.e2e.config.ts` (the real-API suite that self-skips without a key) while `first100-exact-sha.yml` runs the default config, whose `testIncludes` is `*.spec.{ts,tsx}` only. Cases written under the declared name would have greened a cell on a file the greening run never executed. Repointed to `rollback.e2e.spec.ts` through `adjudication.json` `P1-10-F-rollback-e2e-not-yet-created`, BLOCKED-070's sixth application (P4-06, P4-07, P4-08, P4-09, P5-11 preceded it); that suffix enters the default channel and cannot double-run, because the e2e config's include requires a name ending `.e2e.ts`.

FOUR DEFECTS THIS STAGE FOUND IN CODE WHOSE CELLS WERE ALREADY GREEN. Two were PREDICTED from source in the preFlight and then observed RED before either fix, which is the order that makes the prediction worth anything: a migration module throwing on import escaped `resolvePluginUpgrade` verbatim (the plugin's own Error surfacing at `plugin-migration.ts:717`), ending the whole `migrateChangedPlugins` loop and naming nobody; and a module exporting `descriptor` with no `migrate` resolved as `ready` while the guard's own message claimed to require both, failing later as a TypeError inside the transaction with the data already snapshotted. The third was found by measuring rather than predicted: the fencing refusal was ANONYMOUS, because `MigrationRefusal` had no kind that could carry a holder -- it now carries `superseded`, whose holder is read back through `RunLease.currentLease()` rather than derived, so the lease stays the only thing that says who owns the work item, and `undefined` (lapsed, unheld) is reported as the absence it is. The fourth: `recoverUpgrade` throwing took down the whole `dsh plugin update` with a raw stack naming no plugin.

THE RECOVERY RULING, AND WHY IT DIFFERS FROM THE PER-PLUGIN ONE. Before the package manager runs, which plugins it would move is not yet known (`changedVersions` reads that afterwards), so continuing past a plugin left mid-swap risks installing new code onto exactly the half-swapped data acceptance[0] forbids being mismatched. Nothing has moved at that point, so refusing costs nothing and is wholly reversible: an unrecoverable plugin stops the command BY NAME with nothing installed. After the package manager runs the change set IS known, and there the rule is per-plugin isolation. One sentence: nothing uncertain gets past the door while no code has moved; once code has moved, each plugin is cleaned up on its own.

M75 SURVIVED FIRST, AND THAT IS THE MOST USEFUL THING IN THIS ENTRY. The mutation that stops discarding a migrated copy passed the whole suite. It pointed at the CASE rather than the code, per 2.12's rule that a surviving mutation is a question about the instrument: boundary 12 was titled "a materialize that fails DISCARDS its copy" and asserted only the throw and the live unit -- and it could not have asserted a discard, because a failure INSIDE `materializeMigrated` leaves no copy to strand. The behaviour its title named was the one thing that case could never observe. Split into 12 (materialize failed, so no copy exists; asserts no discard happened) and 15 (materialize succeeded, `switchIn` then failed, so a copy exists and must be discarded), after which M75 reddens 15 and only 15.

THE COUNT GUARD IS THE FROZEN TITLE LIST. P4-08.F and P4-11.F guard a DATA table's length; this matrix is fifteen discrete cases, where the equivalent mechanical protection already exists and is already gated -- `expectCases` pins all fifteen titles, so a silently dropped row makes `verify-frozen-titles-in-tree` red. A synthetic guard reading this file's own source would add a second, weaker copy of a check the register already performs (delegate-confirmed).

TWO GREEN-BUT-UNTYPECHECKED DEFECTS, BOTH MINE, BOTH CAUGHT ONLY BY THE REPOSITORY-WIDE TYPECHECK. A new case called `resolvePluginUpgrade` with three arguments where it takes two: the runtime ignored the extra and the case passed for a reason unrelated to what it asserted, and only `pnpm run typecheck` reported TS2554. And `transaction.spec.ts`'s fake lease was missing `currentLease` entirely -- hidden by its `as unknown as RunLease` cast until the product called it, at which point a frozen P case failed with a TypeError. The stub gained the method; the product did NOT gain a `?.()` fallback, which would be defending against a state the typed interface forbids. Both are why a reported SHA carries a repository-wide typecheck and not only a suite.

ONE FROZEN P CASE CHANGED ITS ASSERTION, NOT ITS CRITERION. `REFUSES to switch when this holder was superseded during the migration` keeps its title and now expects `refusal: { kind: 'superseded' }` alongside the outcome it already expected: the behaviour gained information, and the case says the same thing about it. Delegate-approved as an assertion strengthened at F rather than a supersession. P's cell needs re-observation regardless, because this stage edits `transaction.ts`, which P's freeze cites.

entries.note:
The Usage stage, and the stage that gives this epic's compiler a production caller: `RunPlugin` compiles at an agent's FIRST `agent/pre-step`, appends the body to the session log as `run/task-profile`, and names its digest in the Run's `accepted -> planning` transition -- which also makes it P4-01's first production caller of that transition. Every case drives a real turn through a mounted plugin; none calls `compileTaskProfile`, because a case that did would observe the Provider stage again and say nothing about whether anything calls it.

ONE CLAIM WAS WITHDRAWN RATHER THAN FROZEN, and it is recorded here because the absence is deliberate. A case asserting the profile is recorded 'before the step it plans' PASSED with the call moved after `next()`: the loop appends `step/start` and the step's own `user/message` only once the whole pre-step waterfall resolves, so the profile precedes both wherever inside the listener the compile happens, and no log observation distinguishes the two placements. The test file states that instead of asserting it.

TWO ORDERING DECISIONS ARE FROZEN HERE BY THEIR CONSEQUENCES. The body is appended BEFORE the Run is advanced, because the append is synchronous and validates at the append site while `advance` is asynchronous and can refuse; a refusal therefore leaves a profile no Run event names -- inert and self-describing -- rather than a Run event naming a digest whose body never landed. No compensating event is written (delegate ruling, OQ1). And the skip for an unchanged profile (OQ3) is keyed on the profile DIGEST, not on the session-start reason: measured, the reachable case is NOT 'a resume' but a session whose step did not finish, whose durable pending message the resumed agent re-claims with the same id. An ordinary resume claims a new message, yields a new digest, and correctly writes.

Seven mutations, applied locally one at a time to the unmodified tree and reverted between each (`git diff --stat` on the source empty before continuing), then `pnpm exec vitest run packages/run/run --reporter=json` (the OQ2/OQ3/OQ4 three also re-run against `packages/run/task-profile packages/run/run`): (1) the `if (firstStep)` guard on `recordTaskProfile` removed, so every step compiles; (2) `agent.taskProfile = ref` removed; (3) the `advance(runId, 'planning', ...)` call replaced with `void runId`; (4) `origin: taskOriginOf(first.source)` replaced with the constant `'user-goal'`; (5) `goalText` taken from the constant `'a task'` instead of the message; (6) `goalOf`'s non-text tally replaced with `unread: []`, so dropped blocks are silent; (7) the `previousRef !== ref` guard replaced with `previousRef !== ref || true` (append unconditionally) and, separately, with `previousRef === undefined` (never append again).

AN EIGHTH MUTATION WAS RUN AND IS REPORTED BECAUSE IT CAUGHT NOTHING: moving `await this.recordTaskProfile(...)` to AFTER `next()` reddened 0 of 7 cases, which is why the ordering claim above was withdrawn instead of frozen.

A NINTH was abandoned rather than reported as proof: replacing the goal reference's `messageId` with a fixed id reddened 6 of 7, because the undefined `MessageId` import made the listener throw -- a crash, not a value substitution, so it cannot distinguish the case it was meant to probe. entries.note:
The Fault/Qualification stage. THREE CASES THE F preFLIGHT PLANNED ARE DELIBERATELY ABSENT, and the reason is recorded because their absence looks like a gap: a confidence outside [0, 1], both spellings of 'asks about a field it also decided', and a reference that is not a sha256 digest are ALREADY FROZEN IN C, under this same argv. The plan called the third 'C's case re-observed under F's argv', which was the error -- F's argv IS C's, so C's cases run in every F observation and there is nothing to re-observe; a second case carrying an existing title would put two identically named cases in one report and make the title match ambiguous for BOTH entries. The correction is recorded in spec/first100/exec/preflight-P4-02-F.md.

What F adds is what no stage observed. validation[0] and validation[1] in the FAULT direction: each of the four generic kinds compiled from an input that states nothing, asserting the profile asks about all of it and still validates at the durable boundary -- C's four fixtures were literal profiles and P compiled one input. The REFUSAL ORDER, which is itself a claim: a blank injected-context message refuses `not-a-task` and not `empty-goal`, because reporting the second would say a non-task's goal was merely missing and a caller routing on the reason would go looking for text that was never owed; and a whitespace-only goal refuses rather than returning a profile with a blank objective and three questions. And the REVISION ARITHMETIC field by field, which P covered for exactly one field (budget).

validation[2] IS SPLIT ACROSS TWO STAGES by delegate ruling (OQ5, citing the 12.46-B precedent): F freezes the revision arithmetic, which the package suite can observe, and the Usage entry freezes the persistence, which it cannot -- the `run/task-profile` event is written by `@deepseek-ai/dsh-run`. Neither stage claims the whole clause.

sensitivityProof.mutationDescription: The revision-arithmetic block's seven cases are each other's mutation in the strictest available sense -- every one moves one field and asserts the digest moves, with `leaves the reference alone when nothing structured changed` as the positive control that a digest over a clock or a counter would fail. Two further mutations were applied locally and reverted (git diff --stat empty before continuing), then `pnpm exec vitest run packages/run/task-profile packages/run/run --maxWorkers=2 --reporter=json`: (1) in `src/index.ts`, the `unreadContentQuestion` result discarded, which is the only input the tally case reads; (2) in `src/index.ts`, `unreadContentQuestion`'s `.filter(entry => entry.count > 0)` removed.
sensitivityProof.failureSummary: (1) RED 4 of 252, one of them this entry's `changing the tally of content the objective does not include alone changes the reference, so that revision is visible in the chain`; the other three belong to the Provider supplement and the Usage entry. (2) RED 1, in the Provider supplement. The refusal-order pair is proved by each other: the compiler checks `origin` before `goalText`, so swapping those two statements makes `refuses a blank injected-context message as not-a-task, not as empty-goal` report `empty-goal` and redden while the whitespace case stays GREEN -- the two cases cannot both pass under either order. The four-kind block's control is that each asserts `constraints` EMPTY and exactly two questions by FIELD NAME, so a compiler that invented a constraint from the goal text or asked a third thing reddens all four. Mutations reverted.

entries.note: P1-07 U-stage, fifth freeze. One case renamed, none added or removed. The entry's CHARACTERIZATION — that `/trust-skills` cannot grant on a shipped profile because no host user is attached — was true when it was frozen and is false now: P2-01's U2 stage attaches the host user at every local launcher root, so the command reaches approval, the host user confirms, and the clone's skills appear in the catalog. must[2]'s execute half now holds end to end on ONE real boot. entries.note: P2-01 U supplement for the U2 stage (BLOCKED-200, and the delegation half a preFlight census found beside it). Read from the recorded corpus rather than a purpose-built fixture: `snapshots/session/` is what a real `dsh --profile headless` process wrote, so a case there proves the PRODUCT attaches an identity, where a fixture would prove the fixture does. Each claim is a PAIR joined by the actor id, because `action/manifest-appended` records `actor: manifest.actor.id` alone — no kind, no tenant, no chain — while the chain lives on `identity/attached`; the identity half alone would show an identity was attached and nothing about whether actions ran under it. That join is also what acceptance[0]'s 'traceable' means here (§12.85 note 43): from one action you reach the root through its own session log, not through a chain copied into every manifest. `subagent-depth-two-rejection` is the scenario because it carries two hops AND every one of its three logs appends a manifest; `advanced-toolchain` has the same chain shape but its children dispatch no tool, so the actor half would have read `undefined` — which is how the first draft of these cases failed, and why the scenario was chosen by measurement rather than by name. The last case pins OQ30's boundary as counts: 93 of 93 headless logs carry a host identity, 0 of 25 SDK and 0 of 8 ACP, because a request that arrived over a socket is not the machine's host user.

entries.note: P2-05 U supplement for BLOCKED-201, closing BLOCKED-187's input residual with it. `enforceManifestedAction` took the context facts as an optional `Partial` and filled them in place; NEITHER dispatch path passed them, so every policy question a shipped composition ever asked carried `untrusted` and `default` and no `riskClass` at all — a rule about any of them could not match however it was written. The type is required now, the defaulting moved to one reader both paths call, and both paths classify BEFORE appending the manifest so the class is a fact rather than an absence. The same `ActionRiskClassification` goes to `gateActionRisk`, so the policy layer and the risk gate decide about one classification instead of each computing its own. The base bundle's Cedar row holds the kernel hard-deny rule where it held a paragraph explaining why the rule could not be written. entries.note: P2-05 acceptance[2] and acceptance[0]. acceptance[2] is two operations with two answers: Cordis REFUSES a replace (`provide` throws), and does NOT refuse an unmount — the disposer deletes the store entry. What the clause protects is that no Cordis operation converts a denial into permission, so the unmount case drives the SAME action either side of a real dispose and asserts permit-then-deny. This closes the preFlight's OQ1, which recorded the unmount half open because `pinTrustKernel` answers forgery and not loss. acceptance[0]'s five initiators are measured to be one convergence rather than five paths: the PEP has exactly two callers, and subagent, workflow and SDK all obtain an Agent through `ctx.agents.create` whose calls pass `appendToolCall`.

sensitivityProof.mutationDescription: (M1) `composeDecision` stops collecting at the first constraint that does not object — the first-match rule this clause exists to reject, and the one `dsh-permission-rules` actually has. sensitivityProof.failureSummary: M1 reds both 1000-permutation cases AND the two pre-existing order cases — correct, because they assert one property from four angles. M2 reds the silent-only permutation control and its non-permutation sibling, and leaves the two objecting-set permutation cases green, which is the point of having a control: without it those two would pass on a composition that always denied. STATED: 1000 draws from 40320 orderings is a sample, not an exhaustion. The seed makes a failure reproducible; it does not make the coverage complete. An order-dependence that only manifests on orderings this seed never draws would pass.

entries.note: P2-05 validation[1]: the clause asks for 1000 order permutations and the prior evidence was ONE forward/reversed pair. Eight constraints, 1000 seeded draws via mulberry32 from a permit base and an ask base, plus a silent-only control. Seeded rather than `Math.random` because an order-dependent rule that reddens once and passes on re-run is indistinguishable from flake — the exact confusion the clause removes. The constraint MIX is load-bearing: an all-objecting set agrees in every order even under a first-match rule, so silent constraints are interleaved. Cited from acceptance[1] in `acceptance-coverage.json` because `acceptance-coverage.schema.json` indexes acceptance clauses only.
